1. Free Radicals

1.1 What is a free radical?

  • Free radicals are trivalent, neutral carbon species.
  • The radical carbon has 7 e− in its outer shell.
  • They are paramagnetic (one unpaired electron).
  • They are highly unstable and very reactive.
  • They act neither as a Lewis acid nor as a Lewis base.
  • Magnetic moment: μ = √(n(n + 2)) B.M. = √3 B.M. (n = 1)
  • Spin multiplicity = 2|S| + 1 = 2 × ½ + 1 = 2 (doublet).
  • Hybridisation: generally sp2, so they are generally planar. Because of the planar structure a radical can be approached from both sides (top and bottom).
  • CH3• is planar (sp2, odd electron in a p-orbital). CF3• is pyramidal (sp3): the three electronegative F atoms take up the p-character of the C–F bonds, so the odd electron sits in an orbital with more % s.

Bredt’s rule for radicals. A bridgehead radical that must be planar (sp2) in a small rigid bicyclic system does not exist:

sp2 bridgehead radical — does not exist

However, a bridgehead radical that can stay sp3 (pyramidal), here flanked by two O atoms, exists:

sp3 bridgehead radical — exists

1.2 Energy-level diagram of the methyl radical

Radicals are stabilised by conjugating, electron-withdrawing and electron-donating groups. Anything that would stabilise an anion or a cation will also stabilise a radical:

  • electron-withdrawing groups;
  • electron-donating groups (including alkyl groups with C–H σ bonds — hyperconjugation);
  • conjugating groups.

★ 1.3 Shape of radicals

  • •CH3 and simple alkyl radicals: planar (sp2) or a very shallow pyramid that inverts rapidly; the odd electron is in a p orbital.
  • •CF3: pyramidal (≈ sp3), because electronegative F atoms prefer bonds with more p-character, leaving more s-character in the orbital of the odd electron.
  • Allyl, benzyl and Ph3C•: planar, so the p orbital can overlap with the π system (Ph3C• is propeller-shaped because of crowding).
  • Because a planar radical can be attacked from either face, a radical formed at a stereocentre gives a racemic product (see 6.10).

★ 1.4 Stability order of carbon radicals (bond dissociation energies)

The easier it is to break a C–H bond homolytically, the more stable the radical formed. Bond dissociation energies (BDE, kJ mol−1):

Bond brokenRadical formedBDE / kJ mol−1Type
CH2=CH–Hvinyl, CH2=CH•464sp2 (least stable)
CH3–Hmethyl, •CH3439methyl
CH3CH2–Hethyl4201°
(CH3)2CH–Hisopropyl4132°
(CH3)3C–Ht-butyl4003°
PhCH2–Hbenzyl375resonance
CH2=CHCH2–Hallyl369resonance
Ph3C–Htriphenylmethyl339extensive resonance

Order of stability: Ph3C• > allyl ≈ benzyl > 3° > 2° > 1° > •CH3 > vinyl ≈ phenyl.

Why? (i) Hyperconjugation: each α C–H bond donates into the half-filled p orbital (more α-H → more stable). (ii) Resonance: allyl and benzyl radicals spread the odd electron over several atoms. (iii) Vinyl and phenyl radicals keep the odd electron in an sp2 orbital with more s-character, close to the nucleus, so they are the least stable.

★ Verified order: •CH₂F > •CH₃ > •CF₃ (fluorine: donor and acceptor at the same time)

RadicalC–H BDE of the parent / kJ mol−1ShapeMain effect of F
•CH2FH–CH2F 424almost planarone F lone pair donates into the SOMO (+M) — wins over −I
•CHF2H–CHF2 432pyramidaldonation from F still helps, −I grows
•CH3H–CH3 439planarreference
•CF3H–CF3 446strongly pyramidal (σ radical)three F: strong −I; the SOMO gains s-character; lone-pair donation no longer helps

A lower C–H BDE means a more stable radical, so •CH₂F > •CHF₂ > •CH₃ > •CF₃. (BDEs: Luo, Comprehensive Handbook of Chemical Bond Energies, 2007; Blanksby & Ellison 2003.) One fluorine acts like the OR group (see 1.8): its filled 2p orbital overlaps the SOMO (3 electrons in 2 orbitals: net gain). Each extra F pulls σ-electron density (−I) and makes the carbon pyramidal; in •CF₃ the odd electron sits in an orbital with much s-character, the π overlap with the F lone pairs is lost, and the radical is less stable than methyl.

★ What "radical stability" means here

  • Thermodynamic stability = how much energy is needed to make the radical from its parent. It is measured by the C–H bond dissociation energy (BDE): radical-stabilisation energy RSE = BDE(H–CH3) − BDE(H–R). A positive RSE means R• is more stable than •CH3.
  • Kinetic stability (persistence) = how long the radical lives. Bulky groups make a radical persistent without making it thermodynamically stable (for example (t-Bu)3C•).
  • The order •CH2F > •CHF2 > •CH3 > •CF3 is a thermodynamic order based on C–H BDEs. Other reference bonds (R–CH3, R–F) give different numbers for fluorinated radicals, because F also changes the strength of the bond being broken. So this order should not be quoted without saying it is based on C–H BDEs.
RadicalRSE / kJ mol−1 (from C–H BDE)ESR a(13C) / GShape (from ESR)
•CH3038.5planar
•CH2F+1554.8slightly pyramidal
•CHF2+7148.8pyramidal
•CF3−7271.6strongly pyramidal (nearly tetrahedral)

A larger 13C hyperfine coupling a(13C) means more s-character in the SOMO, that is, a more pyramidal carbon (ESR data: Fessenden & Schuler, 1965).

  • One F: the lone-pair donation (+M) is larger than the −I effect, so •CH2F is stabilised (like •CH2OCH3, but less, because the F 2p orbital is very low in energy).
  • Each extra F: −I grows, and the carbon bends (pyramidalises). The SOMO gains s-character, which lowers its energy but weakens the π overlap with the F lone pairs.
  • •CF3: a σ-type radical; lone-pair donation is no longer effective, and −I of three F wins. Its C–H bond (in CF3–H) is stronger than in CH4.
  • Kinetic evidence: •CF3 is a much more reactive (and electrophilic) H-abstractor than •CH3, as expected for a less stable radical that forms a stronger C–H bond.

★ 1.5 Hyperconjugation in the ethyl radical (no-bond resonance)

The σ(C–H) electrons overlap with the singly occupied p orbital. Count the α-H atoms to compare: •CH2CH3 has 3, (CH3)2CH• has 6, (CH3)3C• has 9 hyperconjugating H.

1.7 Stabilisation by electron-withdrawing groups

Let’s first think about what happens when a radical centre is in close proximity to an electron-withdrawing group. Electron-withdrawing groups, such as C=O and C≡N, have a low-lying empty π* orbital. Two new molecular orbitals are produced by overlapping with the radical’s SOMO, which is often a p-orbital. The previous SOMO electron, which is the only electron accessible, can fill either of the two new orbitals. When it enters the new SOMO, which has less energy than the old one, the radical stabilises as a result of the decrease in energy of this electron.

radicals stabilised by functional groups

Stabilisation of a radical by an electron-withdrawing group

1.8 Stabilisation by electron-donating groups

Ether oxygen (OR) has high-energy lone pairs. When the lone-pair (n) orbital interacts with the SOMO, two new MOs form: a new lower-energy filled orbital (holding the two lone-pair electrons) and a new higher-energy SOMO (holding one electron). Two electrons go down in energy and only one goes up, so the system is stabilised overall, even though the SOMO is now higher in energy than before.

Adjacent functional groups weaken C–H bonds: radicals next to carbonyl, nitrile or ether groups, or centred on a carbonyl carbon, are more stable than even tertiary alkyl radicals.

Stabilisation of a radical by an electron-donating group

1.9 Electrophilic and nucleophilic radicals

  • Low-energy SOMOs would rather accept an electron than give one up: radicals next to electron-withdrawing groups are electrophilic.
  • High-energy SOMOs would rather give up an electron: radicals next to electron-donating groups are nucleophilic.

1.10 Captodative effect

Radicals that are stabilised by an electron-withdrawing group and an electron-donating group at the same time are sometimes known as captodative radicals. Special stability of a radical when it is attached to one electron-withdrawing group (−M: C=O, CN) and one electron-donating group (+M: OCH3) at the same time. Such radicals are called captodative radicals (“Most stable — study separately for more details”).

Example. Find the most stable radical.

P(−M, −M)
Q(+M, +M)
R(−M, −M)   S(−M, +M)

Answer: S — captodative effect (one −M and one +M group) makes it the most stable.

★ Why one donor and one acceptor together are special (MO explanation)

A radical next to a donor (D = OR, NR2) and an acceptor (A = C=O, C≡N) on the same carbon is called captodative (capto = accepting, dative = donating). The two effects do more than add up; they reinforce each other (Viehe, 1985):

  • Donor alone: the SOMO mixes with the filled lone-pair orbital n. Two electrons go down and one goes up, so there is net stabilisation, but the new SOMO is higher in energy (1.8).
  • Acceptor alone: the SOMO mixes with the empty π* orbital. The single electron goes down (1.7). The smaller the gap between SOMO and π*, the larger the drop.
  • Both together: the donor first raises the SOMO, which brings it closer to π* of the acceptor. The acceptor now mixes much more strongly and pulls the SOMO down a lot. The odd electron is spread over D, C and A (a 3-centre, 5-electron π system, like the allyl anion with one electron removed).

How big is it? Experimentally the extra stabilisation is real but smaller than early papers claimed, so treat "most stable" as "stabilised by both groups together", not a fixed number.

Example (the one above): S, CH3O–C•H–C≡N, has one +M group and one −M group on the radical carbon, so it is the most stable of P, Q, R and S. P and R have two acceptors; Q has two donors: with two groups of the same kind the second one adds much less.

★ Five captodative radicals, with resonance structures

Each radical below has a π-donor (D: OR, NR2, SR) and a π-acceptor (A: C≡N, C=O) on the radical carbon. Four kinds of structure contribute: the radical on carbon, the odd electron on the acceptor, the donor form (D•+–C−) and the push–pull form D+=C–A•−. The push–pull form is possible only when both groups are present; that is the extra (captodative) stabilisation.

(1)C-centredodd electron on Ndonor formpush–pull form
(2)glycyl radicalodd electron on Opush–pull form
(3)(dimethylamino)cyanomethyl(4)(methylthio)cyanomethyl(5)methoxy(methoxycarbonyl)methyl

Radical (2) is the glycyl radical: the α-C–H of glycine and of the glycine units in proteins is weak for exactly this reason (NH2 donor + COOH acceptor), and some enzymes use a glycyl radical.

Test for a true captodative effect: the radical-stabilisation energy of D–C•–A must be larger than the sum of the values for D–C• and C•–A. Computed and experimental values show a synergy, but it is a few kJ mol−1, not tens. [Not verified]

1.11 How do radicals react?

A reactive radical can (i) combine with another radical to form a spin-paired molecule, (ii) react with a spin-paired molecule to create a new radical, or (iii) undergo a unimolecular process and split into a new radical and a spin-paired molecule.

Order of stability of free radicals

Ph3C• > Ph2CH• > allyl > PhCH2• > 3° alkyl > 2° alkyl > 1° alkyl

•CF3 < •CCl3 (−I effect of F destabilises CF3•; CCl3• is helped by push–pull effect) •CH2F > •CH3 > •CF3

allyl>phenyl radical (σ-radical)>
(+H, hyperconjugation) <(+R, resonance with C=O)
Resonance:

Kinetically stable free radicals

Phenoxyl and anilino radicals with bulky groups (X = t-Bu) at both ortho and para positions do not undergo dimerisation — they are kinetically stable.

2,4,6-tri-tert-butylanilino radical

1.12 The first radical detected

The very first radical to be detected, the triphenylmethyl radical, was made in 1900 (Gomberg) by abstraction of Cl• from Ph3CCl by Ag metal. Many metal atoms such as Ag and Li have single unpaired electrons. This radical is relatively stable but reacts with itself reversibly in solution. The product of dimerisation was for 70 years believed to be hexaphenylethane, but in 1970 NMR showed that it was an unsymmetrical dimer.

Ph3C–ClAgPh3C• (triphenylmethyl)+AgCl
Suggested (1900):hexaphenylethane
Correct (1970):unsymmetrical dimer (quinonoid)

★ 1.13 Solved examples on radical stability

Q1. Arrange in decreasing stability: (a) •CH3 (b) (CH3)3C• (c) PhCH2• (d) CH2=CH•

Solution. c > b > a > d. Benzyl is resonance-stabilised; t-butyl has 9 hyperconjugating H; methyl has none; vinyl keeps the odd electron in an sp2 orbital.

Q2. Which C–H bond of 3-methyl-1-butene breaks most easily on homolysis?

Solution. The C-3 hydrogen: it is both tertiary and allylic, so the radical (CH3)2C•–CH=CH2 is stabilised by resonance and by 6 α-H.

Q3. Which is more stable: cyclopropylmethyl radical or the cyclobutyl radical? Why does the first one ring-open?

Solution. Cyclopropylmethyl (•CH2–C3H5) is a 1° radical and the ring is strained; it opens extremely fast (k ≈ 108 s−1) to the but-3-enyl radical CH2=CH–CH2–CH2•. This "radical clock" is used to test whether a reaction goes through radicals.

Q4. Ph3C• exists in solution in equilibrium with its dimer. Give two reasons it does not dimerise completely.

Solution. (1) The odd electron is delocalised over three rings (very stable radical). (2) The three phenyl rings make the central carbon crowded, so the C–C bond of the dimer would be weak.

★ 1.14 Very hard solved examples: structure and stability of radicals

Q1. Arrange the C–H bonds in order of increasing bond dissociation energy: (a) H–CH2CH=CH2 (b) H–C≡CH (c) H–C6H5 (d) H–CH2C6H5 (e) H–C(CH3)3.

Solution. a < d < e < c < b (≈ 371, 375, 404, 472, 558 kJ mol−1). Allyl and benzyl radicals are resonance-stabilised (almost equal). t-Butyl is stabilised by 9 α-C–H hyperconjugation. Phenyl and ethynyl radicals keep the odd electron in an sp2 / sp orbital (no resonance, high s-character), so those C–H bonds are the strongest.

Q2. Arrange in decreasing stability: Ph3C•, Ph2CH•, PhCH2•, CH2=CH–CH2•, (CH3)3C•.

Solution. Ph3C• > Ph2CH• > PhCH2• ≈ CH2=CH–CH2• > (CH3)3C•. Each extra phenyl adds delocalisation (C–H BDE ≈ 339, 354, 375, 371, 404 kJ). The gain from the 2nd and 3rd phenyl is smaller than from the 1st because the rings cannot all be coplanar (propeller shape).

Q3. Which is the least stable: 1-propyl, 2-propyl or cyclopropyl radical? Explain.

Solution. Cyclopropyl. The 60° ring cannot let the radical carbon become planar, so the odd electron sits in an orbital with much s-character (a σ radical) and gets no hyperconjugative help. Making it costs more energy: c-C3H5–H ≈ 445 kJ mol−1, against 423 (1°) and 413 (2°). Order of stability: 2-propyl > 1-propyl > cyclopropyl.

Q4. Count the hyperconjugative (no-bond) structures of (a) 2-methylbut-2-yl radical, (CH3)2C•–CH2CH3, and (b) 3-methylbut-2-yl radical, CH3–C•H–CH(CH3)2. Which is more stable?

Solution. (a) α-H atoms: 3 + 3 + 2 = 8 structures. (b) α-H atoms: 3 (CH3) + 1 (CH) = 4. So (a), a 3° radical, is more stable, as expected.

Q5. CH3• is planar but CF3• is clearly pyramidal. Explain.

Solution. Fluorine is very electronegative, so the C–F bonds take more p-character (Bent's rule) and leave more s-character for the orbital holding the odd electron; an orbital with s-character points out of the plane, so the radical becomes pyramidal (like sp3). Repulsion between the F lone pairs and the odd electron also favours bending.

Q6. A bridgehead radical (1-norbornyl) forms easily, but the 1-norbornyl cation is extremely hard to make. Why the difference?

Solution. A carbocation needs a planar centre so that its empty p orbital is not mixed with s-character; the cage forces a pyramid, so the cation is very unstable. A radical has only a small energy preference for planarity (it can be a shallow pyramid), so the pyramidal bridgehead radical costs little energy.

Q7. How many lines appear in the ESR spectrum of (a) •CH3 (b) CH3CH2• (c) (CH3)2CH• (d) (CH3)3C•? (Use the n + 1 rule for each set of equivalent H.)

Solution. (a) 3 H → 4 lines (1 : 3 : 3 : 1). (b) 2 α-H and 3 β-H with different couplings → 3 × 4 = 12 lines. (c) 1 α-H and 6 β-H → 2 × 7 = 14 lines. (d) 9 equivalent β-H → 10 lines.

Q8. Which alkene reacts faster with the t-butyl radical, CH2=CH–CN or CH2=CH–OC2H5? Which reacts faster with the CF3• radical?

Solution. (CH3)3C• is nucleophilic (electron-rich, 3 alkyl donors): it adds much faster to the electron-poor CH2=CH–CN. CF3• is electrophilic: it adds faster to the electron-rich enol ether CH2=CH–OEt. Both add to the CH2 end so as to give the more stabilised radical.

Q9. Why is cyclohexa-1,4-diene an excellent H-atom donor, even better than toluene?

Solution. Removing one doubly allylic H gives the cyclohexadienyl radical (spread over 5 carbons). This radical easily loses its second H to give benzene, so the overall loss of 2H is driven by aromatisation. The first C–H BDE is only about 320 kJ mol−1.

Q10. Rank the stability of •CH2–CH3, •CH2–CN, •CH2–OCH3 and •CH(CN)(OCH3).

Solution. •CH(CN)(OCH3) > •CH2–CN ≈ •CH2–OCH3 > •CH2–CH3. Both an electron-withdrawing group (CN, by delocalisation) and a donor (OCH3, lone-pair interaction) stabilise a radical; one of each on the same carbon gives an extra "captodative" stabilisation (1.10).

Q11. Vinyl radicals made from (E)- and (Z)-1-bromoprop-1-ene with Bu3SnD give the same E/Z mixture of 1-deuterioprop-1-ene. What does this tell you about vinyl radicals?

Solution. The vinyl radical is bent (σ radical) but inverts very fast between the two bent forms, faster than it takes D from Bu3SnD. So the starting geometry is forgotten, and both bromides give the same product mixture.

Q12. TEMPO (2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidin-1-oxyl) is stable for years. Give two structural reasons and say why it is used to "count" radicals.

Solution. (1) The odd electron is shared between N and O (a 2-centre, 3-electron N–O bond). (2) Both α-carbons carry two methyl groups: no α-H, so it cannot disproportionate, and dimerisation (O–O) is blocked by bulk and is weak. TEMPO couples rapidly with carbon radicals (R–O–N<), so trapping R• with TEMPO proves that radicals were present.

2. Generation of Free Radicals

2.1 Thermolysis (pyrolysis)

On heating, weak bonds such as Cl–Cl, O–O and N=N break homolytically to give free radicals. Cyclopropane, on heating, ring-opens to a 1,3-diradical. Peroxides (ROOR or (PhCOO)2) readily undergo homolysis of the O–O bond.

(a) Cl–Cl Δ 2Cl•

(b) (CH3)3C–Cl Δ (CH3)3C• + Cl•

(c) R–O–O–R Δ 2RO•

(d)Δ1,3-diradical

(e) Ph–CO–O–O–CO–Ph Δ 2PhCOO•

★ 2.2 Bond energies of common initiators

BondBDE / kJ mol−1Comment
RO–OR (peroxides)≈ 150breaks at 80–130 °C
F–F159very weak; F2 reacts explosively
Cl–Cl243needs light (hν) or heat
Br–Br193visible light is enough
I–I151breaks easily but I• is too unreactive
C–N=N–C (AIBN)—N2 loss is driven by entropy and the strong N≡N bond

Half-life temperature (10 h): AIBN ≈ 65 °C < benzoyl peroxide ≈ 73 °C < di-t-butyl peroxide ≈ 125 °C. So AIBN is used for low-temperature reactions.

2.3 Redox reactions

In redox reactions, radicals are formed by single-electron transfer (SET), i.e. by removal or addition of one electron.

(a) (ArCOO)2 + Cu+ ⟶ ArCOO• + ArCOO− + Cu2+

(b) ArN2+ + Cu+ ⟶ Ar• + N2 + Cu2+

(c) H2O2 + Fe2+ ⟶ HO• + OH− + Fe3+ (Fenton reaction)

Photolysis uses the energy of photons for homolytic cleavage. The bond breaks homolytically when the energy of the light is equal to or greater than the bond dissociation energy.

2.14 Decomposition of diacyl peroxides / peroxy esters — three mechanisms

General structure: R1–C(=O)–O–O–R2. In peroxy (O–O) compounds, different C–O and O–O bonds can break, depending on the weakest bond, the stability of the radicals formed and the driving force (formation of CO2, a carbonyl compound, tertiary/benzylic radicals).

Mechanism 1 — O–O homolysis (one bond): R1–CO–O–O–R2 Δ or hν R1–CO–O• (acyloxy radical) + •O–R2 (alkoxy radical)

Mechanism 2 — fragmentation with decarboxylation (two bonds): R1–CO–O–O– R2 Δ or hν R1• + CO2 + •O–R2

Mechanism 3 — cleavage of three bonds [R1–C(=O), C(=O)–O and O–R2]: R1–CO– O–O–R2 Δ or hν R1• + CO2 + •R2

★ 2.17 Solved examples on generating radicals

Q1. Which initiator would you choose for a radical reaction at 60–70 °C: (a) di-t-butyl peroxide (b) AIBN (c) Cl2 in the dark?

Solution. (b) AIBN. Di-t-butyl peroxide needs > 120 °C; Cl2 needs light.

Q2. Write the radicals formed when di-t-butyl peroxide is heated, and what one of them can give by β-scission.

Solution. (CH3)3CO–OC(CH3)3 ⟶ 2 (CH3)3CO•; then (CH3)3CO• ⟶ CH3COCH3 + •CH3 (see 3.8).

Q3. Why does Bu3SnH with AIBN reduce R–Br to R–H?

Solution. AIBN gives (CH3)2C•CN, which takes H from Bu3Sn–H. Bu3Sn• + R–Br ⟶ Bu3SnBr + R• (strong Sn–Br bond); R• + Bu3Sn–H ⟶ R–H + Bu3Sn• (chain).

★ 2.18 Very hard solved examples: generating radicals

Q1. What is the longest wavelength of light that can break (a) Cl–Cl (243 kJ mol−1) (b) Br–Br (193) (c) I–I (151) (d) CH3–H (439)? (NAhc = 0.1196 J m mol−1.)

Solution. λ = NAhc / E. (a) 0.1196 / 243 000 = 4.92 × 10−7 m = 492 nm (blue). (b) 620 nm (orange-red, visible light is enough). (c) 792 nm (near IR). (d) 272 nm (far UV). This is why Cl2 and Br2 are split by ordinary light but C–H is not.

Q2. AIBN has a 10-hour half-life at 65 °C (first order). What fraction decomposes in the first hour at 65 °C? How long for 90%?

Solution. Fraction left after 1 h = (½)1/10 = 0.933, so 6.7% decomposes. For 90% decomposition: t = 10 h × log2 10 = 10 × 3.32 = 33 h. So a radical reaction at 65 °C has a slow, steady supply of radicals.

Q3. Azomethane, CH3–N=N–CH3, needs about 400 °C to decompose, but AIBN decomposes at 65 °C. Explain.

Solution. Both lose N2 to give two radicals. AIBN gives 2 (CH3)2C•–CN: 3° and stabilised by the C≡N π system, so the transition state for C–N cleavage is much lower. Azomethane gives the unstabilised CH3•.

Q4. t-Butyl peresters RC(=O)O–OC(CH3)3 decompose faster when R = PhCH2 than when R = CH3, by a large factor. Explain.

Solution. With R = CH3 only the O–O bond breaks first (one-bond homolysis) and CH3CO2• loses CO2 later. With R = PhCH2 the O–O and R–CO2 bonds break together (concerted two-bond fission), because the benzyl radical formed is stabilised; this lowers Eₐ. (A larger effect is seen with Ph2CH and Ph3C.)

Q5. Silver (S)-2-methylbutanoate reacts with Br2 (Hunsdiecker reaction). Give the product and its optical activity. What does this prove?

Solution. RCOOAg + Br2 ⟶ RCOOBr + AgBr; RCOO–Br ⟶ RCOO• + Br•; RCOO• ⟶ R• + CO2; R• + RCOOBr ⟶ R–Br + RCOO•. R• = sec-butyl (planar), so the product is racemic 2-bromobutane (optically inactive). Loss of configuration shows a free radical intermediate.

Q6. Fe2+ + H2O2 (Fenton's reagent) converts benzene into phenol. Give the steps.

Solution. Fe2+ + H2O2 ⟶ Fe3+ + HO− + HO•. HO• adds to the ring to give the hydroxycyclohexadienyl radical. Fe3+ oxidises it to the cation, which loses H+ to give phenol (rearomatisation). Iron is a redox catalyst for making the radical.

Q7. Cumene (isopropylbenzene) is oxidised by air to cumene hydroperoxide, which with acid gives phenol + acetone. Write the radical chain for the first part.

Solution. Initiation: In• + PhC(CH3)2–H ⟶ In–H + PhC•(CH3)2 (3° and benzylic). Propagation: PhC•(CH3)2 + O2 ⟶ PhC(CH3)2–OO•; PhC(CH3)2–OO• + PhC(CH3)2H ⟶ PhC(CH3)2–OOH + PhC•(CH3)2. Only the tertiary benzylic H reacts, because the ROO• radical is quite selective.

Q8. Why do old bottles of diisopropyl ether and THF become explosive?

Solution. The C–H next to oxygen is weak (the radical is stabilised by an O lone pair). Air slowly oxidises it by autoxidation to α-hydroperoxides and polymeric peroxides, which explode on heating or concentration. Diisopropyl ether is worst: its α-H is also 3°.

Q9. Lithium enolate of acetophenone treated with CuCl2 gives a C16 compound. What is it?

Solution. One-electron oxidation of the enolate gives the radical PhCOCH2•; two of these combine: PhCOCH2–CH2COPh (1,4-diphenylbutane-1,4-dione), a 1,4-diketone. Oxidation of an anion is a radical-generating method (2.11).

Q10. Why is a radical initiator needed only in catalytic amounts (about 1 mol %) in a chain reaction, but in a full equivalent in a non-chain reaction such as Kolbe electrolysis?

Solution. In a chain each initiating radical is regenerated in the propagation steps and makes hundreds or thousands of product molecules before termination. Kolbe coupling is a non-chain process: every product needs two radicals made at the electrode.

Q11. Tetraethyllead was added to petrol. What radicals does it give, and why was it effective in small amounts?

Solution. Pb(C2H5)4 ⟶ Pb + 4 C2H5• on heating (the Pb–C bond is weak). The ethyl radicals (and the lead oxides formed) remove the reactive radicals and peroxides that would set off early, uncontrolled ignition (knock). One molecule interrupts many chains.

Q12. Why is DPPH (2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl) used to test for radical scavenging (antioxidant activity)?

Solution. DPPH is a persistent, deep-violet radical. When an antioxidant gives it an H atom it becomes the pale-yellow hydrazine DPPH–H. The fall in the violet colour (measured at ≈ 517 nm) shows how many radicals were trapped.

3. Reactions of Free Radicals

3.1 Combination (coupling)

Two radicals combine by forming a new σ-bond. This is a common mode of termination of a radical chain reaction. In the absence of a reagent, radicals combine (dimerise) to give R2 (e.g. 2CH3• → C2H6).

(a) CH3• + Cl• ⟶ CH3–Cl

(b) Br• + Br• ⟶ Br2

A biradical is an intermediate with two unpaired electrons. It can form during radical reactions and undergoes intramolecular combination to give a π-bond or a cyclic product (ring closure).

3.3 Disproportionation

Two radicals can also react by disproportionation: one radical (the acceptor) takes an H atom from the carbon next to the radical centre (the β-H) of the other radical (the donor). The donor becomes an alkene and the acceptor becomes an alkane. Disproportionation competes with combination; both happen together, and disproportionation becomes more important when the donor has many β-H atoms and when the radical centres are crowded. [Corrected]

General trend: more β-H atoms and more crowding → more disproportionation → less dimerisation (combination). [Corrected]

3.6 Reactivity of phenoxy radicals

Phenoxy radicals are resonance stabilised: the unpaired electron is delocalised at the o-and p-positions. Hence they usually do not undergo rearrangement; instead coupling (C– C or C–O) occurs.

Mechanism (oxidative coupling): phenol NaOH phenoxide K3Fe(CN)6 phenoxy radical.

★ 3.7 Radical cyclisation (5-exo-trig)

5-hexenyl radicalk ≈ 2 × 105 s−1cyclopentylmethyl radical

The 5-hexenyl radical closes to the five-membered ring (5-exo) faster than to the six-membered ring (6-endo), even though the 6-endo product is the more stable 2° radical: the 5-exo transition state has better orbital overlap.

★ 3.8 β-Scission (fragmentation) of alkoxy radicals

The C–C bond β to the oxygen breaks because a strong C=O π bond forms. When there is a choice, the most stable radical is lost: (CH3)2C(Et)O• loses •C2H5 faster than •CH3. This is also why the hypochlorite in 6.6 (example 3) gives acetone.

★ 3.9 Radical rearrangements: the 1,2-aryl shift (neophyl rearrangement)

neophyl radical (1°)1,2-Ph shift2-methyl-1-phenylprop-2-yl radical (3°)

Unlike carbocations, alkyl radicals do not undergo 1,2-H or 1,2-alkyl shifts. Aryl (and vinyl) groups can shift because they move through a cyclopropane-type (spiro) intermediate in which the odd electron is delocalised over the ring.

★ 3.10 Solved examples on radical reactions

Q1. Give all products formed when a mixture of ethyl and isopropyl radicals terminates.

Solution. Combination: butane, 2-methylbutane, 2,3-dimethylbutane. Disproportionation: ethane + propene, propane + ethene, ethane + ethene, propane + propene.

Q2. Predict the main product of Bu3SnH/AIBN with 6-bromohex-1-ene.

Solution. R• = 5-hexenyl, which cyclises before it can take H from Bu3SnH (at low [Bu3SnH]): the main product is methylcyclopentane; at high [Bu3SnH] some hex-1-ene forms.

Q3. Why does the triphenylmethyl radical "dimer" have a quinonoid structure instead of hexaphenylethane?

Solution. Coupling at the crowded central carbons is blocked, so one Ph3C• bonds through the para carbon of a ring of the other radical (Jacobson structure).

★ 3.11 Very hard solved examples: what radicals do

Q1. A mixture of •CH3 and (CH3)3C• terminates. List every product.

Solution. Combination: C2H6, (CH3)4C (neopentane), (CH3)3C–C(CH3)3. Disproportionation: (CH3)3C• donates a β-H to CH3•: CH4 + CH2=C(CH3)2; two t-Bu radicals: (CH3)3CH + CH2=C(CH3)2. CH3• can never donate (no β-H), so there is no "t-BuH + CH2" pair.

Q2. Give all products of termination of two sec-butyl radicals, CH3–C•H–CH2CH3, including stereoisomers.

Solution. Combination: 3,4-dimethylhexane as meso + (±). Disproportionation: acceptor gives butane; donor can lose a β-H from C-1 (but-1-ene) or from C-3 (but-2-ene, both E and Z).

Q3. For ethyl radicals kd/kc = 0.14. What percentage of ethyl radical encounters gives butane? If 1 mol of ethyl radicals reacts, how many moles of ethene form?

Solution. Fraction combining = 1/1.14 = 87.7%; disproportionating = 12.3%. 1 mol radicals = 0.5 mol encounters; 0.5 × 0.123 = 0.061 mol ethene (and 0.061 mol ethane), with 0.439 mol butane.

Q4. The crotyl radical CH3CH=CH–CH2• dimerises. How many constitutional isomers of C8H14 form? Name them.

Solution. The radical is delocalised: CH3CH=CH–CH2• ⟷ CH3C•H–CH=CH2. Bonding through the CH2 end (head) or the CH(CH3) end (tail): head–head: octa-2,6-diene; head–tail: 3-methylhepta-1,5-diene; tail–tail: 3,4-dimethylhexa-1,5-diene. Three constitutional isomers (plus E/Z and stereoisomers).

Q5. (Bromomethyl)cyclopropane is treated with Bu3SnH/AIBN. What is the main product, and why is this reaction called a "radical clock"?

Solution. Cyclopropylmethyl radical opens very fast (k ≈ 108 s−1) to CH2=CH–CH2–CH2•, which takes H from Bu3SnH: but-1-ene. Only at very high [Bu3SnH] is some methylcyclopropane seen. The ratio of ring-opened to unopened product, with the known k, times how fast the H-transfer is.

Q6. The 5-methylhex-5-enyl radical, •CH2CH2CH2CH2C(CH3)=CH2, cyclises mainly to a six-membered ring, unlike the parent 5-hexenyl radical. Explain.

Solution. In 5-exo closure the radical must attack C-5, which now carries the CH3 group: this is sterically hindered and slowed a lot. 6-endo attack is at the unhindered CH2 and gives a 3° radical (methylcyclohexyl). So the 6-endo product becomes the major one.

Q7. Photolysis of pentan-2-one gives acetone + ethene and also a cyclobutanol. Explain by a biradical.

Solution. The excited C=O oxygen takes a γ-H through a 6-membered TS (Norrish type II, 1,5-H shift) to give a 1,4-biradical: CH3C•(OH)–CH2–CH2–C•H2. It either (a) breaks the central C–C bond: CH2=CH2 + CH3C(OH)=CH2 (enol → acetone), or (b) the two radical centres combine: 1-methylcyclobutan-1-ol (Yang cyclisation).

Q8. An alkoxy radical CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2O• (from a nitrite by light, Barton reaction) gives a δ-functionalised product. Which carbon becomes a radical?

Solution. The O• takes an H from C-4 (δ) through a six-membered TS (1,5-H shift): HOCH2CH2CH2C•HCH3. The new 2° carbon radical is then trapped by NO, giving a nitroso compound that tautomerises to an oxime.

Q9. Neopentyl bromide is treated (a) with Bu3SnH/AIBN and (b) with AgNO3 in ethanol. Give the main organic product of each.

Solution. (a) Radical: (CH3)3C–CH2• does not rearrange (alkyl radicals do not do 1,2-methyl shifts), so the product is neopentane. (b) Ag+ pulls off Br−; the 1° cation (or the ionising C–Br bond) undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift to the 3° tert-pentyl cation: 2-methylbut-2-ene and ethyl tert-pentyl ether.

Q10. Two 1-phenylethyl radicals (PhC•HCH3), made from optically pure (S)-1-bromo-1-phenylethane, combine. What stereoisomers of 2,3-diphenylbutane form?

Solution. The radical is planar, so its stereocentre is lost. Combination gives (R,R), (S,S) and meso in about 1 : 1 : 2 (statistical). The product is optically inactive. (Disproportionation also gives styrene + ethylbenzene.)

Q11. Why does 2,4,6-tri-t-butylphenoxyl radical stay blue in solution for weeks, while the phenoxy radical from phenol couples in seconds?

Solution. Coupling of phenoxyl radicals happens at O, ortho-C and para-C. In 2,4,6-tri-t-butylphenoxyl all three sites carrying spin are blocked by t-butyl groups, so it cannot dimerise; it is a persistent radical (steric protection, plus delocalisation).

Q12. p-Cresol oxidised with alkaline K3Fe(CN)6 gives "Pummerer's ketone". Which radical positions couple?

Solution. The p-cresol phenoxyl radical has spin at O, the two ortho carbons and the para carbon (which carries CH3). ortho-C of one radical couples with para-C of the other; the para-coupled ring becomes a cyclohexadienone (it has no H to lose), and the OH of the other ring then adds to the dienone (Michael addition) to close a furan ring.

4. General Methods of Preparation (GMP) of Alkanes

4.1 Wurtz reaction

Alkyl halides are boiled with Na in dry ether to obtain a hydrocarbon.

R–X + 2Na + X–R Boildry ether R–R + 2NaX

Mechanism

(1) Free-radical mechanism: 2Na + 2R–X RDS 2NaX + 2R•; R• + R• ⟶ R–R

(2) Ionic mechanism: 2Na + R–X ⟶ R−Na+; R−Na+ + R–X ⟶ R–R + NaX (SN2). With 3° R–X, the E2 product forms instead.

(i) Metal (electron transfer):R–X + 2 NaR− Na+ + NaX
(ii) SN2 (carbanion attacks):  R:−  +  R′–C–XR–R′ + X−

Important points

  • Free-radical and carbanion intermediates are both observed.
  • C–X bond breaking is involved in the RDS, so reactivity: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F.
  • CH4 can never be obtained by the Wurtz reaction.
  • A hydrocarbon with an odd number of carbons cannot be obtained in good yield: two different halides give a mixture of three alkanes (R–R, R′–R′, R–R′) that is hard to separate.
  • Dihalides give rings (intramolecular coupling). Halides with more than 6 carbons between the halogens undergo polymerisation instead of cyclisation.

Examples

★ Wurtz reaction with mixed halides

CH3Br + C2H5BrNadry etherCH3–CH3 + CH3–C2H5 + C2H5–C2H5

A mixture of two alkyl halides gives three alkanes, which are hard to separate, so the Wurtz reaction is used mainly for symmetrical alkanes (R–R, even number of C). Methane cannot be made by the Wurtz reaction.

Q1. How many alkanes form when a mixture of 1-bromopropane and 2-bromopropane is treated with Na/dry ether? Name them.

Solution. Three: hexane (n-Pr + n-Pr), 2-methylpentane (n-Pr + i-Pr) and 2,3-dimethylbutane (i-Pr + i-Pr).

Q2. Which alkane cannot be made in good yield by the Wurtz reaction: (a) butane (b) 2,3-dimethylbutane (c) propane (d) hexane?

Solution. (c) propane (odd number of C, needs CH3X + C2H5X, which gives a mixture).

★ Wurtz reaction step by step (radical path): is it a chain?

No. The Wurtz reaction is a non-chain radical reaction: every R• is made by an electron from the sodium surface, and the products are formed by the same steps that end a chain (combination, disproportionation). So there is no propagation step that regenerates a radical.

StepEquationComment
Electron transfer (start)R–X + Na ⟶ R• + Na+X−single electron transfer (SET) from the metal; C–X breaks
Electron transfer (2nd)R• + Na ⟶ R−Na+a second SET gives the carbanion (organosodium)
Coupling (ionic)R−Na+ + R–X ⟶ R–R + NaXSN2; main route to R–R for 1° halides
Coupling (radical)R• + •R ⟶ R–Rradical combination (termination-type step)
Side reaction2 CH3CH2• ⟶ CH3CH3 + CH2=CH2disproportionation
Side reactionR− + H–CH2–CH2–X ⟶ R–H + CH2=CH2 + X−E2 by the carbanion (main path for 3° R–X)

Evidence for radicals: ethane and ethene accompany butane in the Wurtz reaction of ethyl halides, and a 5-hexenyl halide gives some methylcyclopentane (radical cyclisation, see 3.7).

Competing products: alkane + alkene (disproportionation, E2 by R−), and with two different halides a mixture R–R, R–R′, R′–R′.

4.4 Ullmann reaction

The Ullmann reaction is an organic reaction used to couple two molecules of aryl halide to form a biaryl using copper metal and thermal conditions: Ar–I CuΔ Ar–Ar + I2. The mechanism for the Ullmann reaction is not fully understood, but there are two popular mechanisms. The radical mechanism begins with a single electron transfer (SET) from the copper metal to the aryl halide to form an aryl radical. Two aryl radicals then react to form the final biaryl product. The second proposed mechanism begins with oxidative addition of the copper to the aryl halide followed by a SET to form an organocopper reagent. The organocopper performs another oxidative addition on an aryl halide and after reductive elimination results in the final biaryl product. The Ullmann reaction mechanism is not fully understood; the two most popular mechanisms are shown below.

  • (A) Radical mechanism: single-electron transfer (SET) from Cu to the aryl halide gives an aryl radical (+ Cu–X). Two aryl radicals couple to give the biaryl.
  • (B) Aryl-copper mechanism: oxidative addition of Cu(0) to Ar–X gives aryl copper Ar–Cu(II)X; a second oxidative addition of Ar–X gives Ar–Cu(III)X2–Ar, and reductive elimination gives Ar–Ar + Cu(I)X.
(A) SET (radical path):Ar–ICu, SETAr• + CuI
Coupling:2 Ar•Ar–Ar
(B) Ar–Cu (oxidative addition):Ar–I + CuAr–Cu–I+Ar–IAr–Ar + CuI2
CuΔ1,8-naphthyl diradical+perylene

The electron-withdrawing NO2 group makes oxidative addition of Cu into Ar–I easier; Ar–I is the weakest aryl–halogen bond.

4.5 Kolbe’s electrolytic synthesis (KES)

Electrolysis of an aqueous solution of the sodium or potassium salt of a fatty acid gives a higher hydrocarbon: 2RCOONa Electrolysis R–R. (Anode = oxidation, cathode = reduction: “An Ox, Red Cat”.)

Step 1(anode: oxidation)2 RCOO−−2e−2 RCOO•
Step 2(decarboxylation)
Step 3(coupling)R• + •RR–R (alkane at anode; H2 + OH− at cathode)

At anode:

  • 2RCOO− ⟶ 2R–COO• + 2e−

  • 2R• ⟶ R–R

At cathode (reduction of water): 2H2O + 2e− ⟶ H2↑ + 2OH−; Na+ + OH− ⟶ NaOH

  • Free-radical intermediate.
  • Gases at anode: CO2, and R–R (if up to 4 carbons). Gas at cathode: H2.
  • pH increases as the reaction progresses (NaOH forms).
  • CH4 cannot be obtained.
  • Side product: RCOO• + R• ⟶ RCOOR (ester).

Q5. Make 2-methylhexane by Corey–House. Which pair is better: (a) (i-Pr)2CuLi + 1-bromobutane, or (b) (n-Bu)2CuLi + 2-bromopropane?

Solution. (a). The coupling step is SN2-like, so the alkyl halide should be 1° (or methyl). The cuprate can carry a 1°, 2° or 3° group.

Q6. Why is Corey–House better than Wurtz for unsymmetrical alkanes?

Solution. Only the cross product R–R′ forms (no R–R or R′–R′), and odd-carbon alkanes are easy to make.

★ Mechanism of the Corey–House coupling

StepEquationComment
Step 1R–X + 2Li ⟶ R–Li + LiXin dry ether
Step 22 R–Li + CuI ⟶ R2Cu−Li+ + LiIlithium dialkylcuprate (Gilman reagent)
Step 3R2Cu− + R′–X ⟶ [R2Cu(R′)X]− (Cu(III))SN2-like oxidative addition: back-side attack, inversion at the carbon of R′

★ SN2 or E2? (drawn)

1° halide+(CH3)2CuLietherbutane: SN2 coupling
2° halide+(CH3)2CuLiether2-methylbutane (major, SN2)+but-2-ene+but-1-ene (minor, E2)
3° halide+(CH3)2CuLietherisobutene (E2, major) no neopentane
[(CH3)3C]2CuLi +1° halideether2,2-dimethylbutane(the 3° group must be on copper)

Rule: the halide R′–X should be methyl or 1° (2° works, with some E2 and inversion); a 3° halide gives the E2 alkene because the cuprate acts as a base. The cuprate itself may carry 1°, 2°, 3°, vinyl or aryl groups.

★ Corey–House: the three stages drawn

Stage 11-bromobutane+2 Lidry ether−10 °Cbutyllithium+LiBr
Stage 22+CuIether/THF−78 → 0 °Clithium dibutylcuprate (Gilman reagent)+LiI
Stage 3+CH₃Brether0 °Cpentane+butylcopper+LiBr
  • Stage 1 is itself a metal-surface reaction: two single-electron transfers from Li (R–X ⟶ R• ⟶ R−Li+).
  • Only one of the two R groups of R2CuLi is used; the other ends up as RCu. So the cuprate is made from the cheaper halide.
  • Accepted mechanism and its limits: for methyl, 1° and most 2° halides, the evidence (inversion at a 2° carbon, rate order I > Br > Cl, faster for less hindered R′X) fits an SN2-like attack of copper on carbon (oxidative addition to Cu(III)) followed by reductive elimination. With some 2° iodides partial racemisation shows that single-electron-transfer (radical) paths also take part. Vinyl and aryl halides cannot react by back-side SN2; they couple through oxidative addition at the C–X bond, and vinyl halides keep their C=C geometry.

Summary: the halide partner works best as CH3, 1°, allylic, benzylic, vinyl or aryl (iodide or bromide). 2° gives coupling with some E2; 3° and neopentyl give little or no coupling. The group on copper can be 1°, 2°, 3°, vinyl or aryl. With allylic halides SN2 and SN2′ products can both form; the ratio depends on the substrate and conditions.

4.8 Decarboxylation of carboxylic acids (soda lime)

A carboxylic acid (or its salt), when heated with soda lime (CaO + NaOH), undergoes decarboxylation: RCOOH or RCOONa CaO + NaOHΔ RH

ThenR− + H2O (or Na+ OH−)R–H + OH−

Q. Arrange in increasing order of rate of decarboxylation (compare carbanion stability).

(1) a: CH3CH2COONa, b: CH3(CH2)2COONa, c: CH3(CH2)3COONa. Carbanions:

CH3CH2− is more stable than larger 1° carbanions (+I). Ans: c < b < a

(2)a:b:— cyclopropyl carbanion (more s-character) > cyclobutyl carbanion. Ans: b < a
(3)a:b:— carbanion from a is α to C=O (resonance stabilised, enolate). Ans: b < a
(4)a:b:— bridgehead carbanion in a cannot overlap with C=O (Bredt), while b gives an enolate. Ans: a < b
(5)a:b:— carbanion of b is more delocalised (pentadienyl > allyl). Ans: a < b

Groups that promote decarboxylation

Decarboxylation is promoted by any factor that increases the stability of the resulting carbanion because the formation of a carbanion is the key step of decarboxylation. Therefore, electron-attracting groups in R that could stabilize the carbanion by delocalizing the negative charge are expected to promote decarboxylation. It thus follows that acids with electron-attracting groups, such as –NO2, –C≡N, >CO, –CX3, etc. attached to the α-carbon (proper position to accept the C–C bonding electrons) decarboxylate quite easily. The corresponding carboxylate anions (e.g., CH3COCH2COO−, O2NCH2COO−, Cl3CCH2COO− etc.) thus undergo readily decarboxylation because the resulting carbanions are considerably stabilized. For example:

2-Nitropropanoate

Δ−CO2; slow [CH3CH=N+(O−)2 ⟷ CH3C−H–NO2] H+(solvent) CH3CH2NO2 (nitroethane)

3,3,3-Trifluoropropanoate

Δ−CO2; slow F3C–CH2− (stabilised by strong −I of CF3) H+ F3CCH3 (1,1,1-trifluoroethane)

★ Why both NaOH and CaO? Uses of soda-lime decarboxylation

ComponentFunction
NaOH (the real reagent)turns the acid into its carboxylate (RCOO−Na+), supplies the base that removes CO2 as Na2CO3, and provides the H that ends up on R (via water/OH−).
CaOkeeps the mixture dry (NaOH is deliquescent), stops NaOH from melting and attacking the glass tube, keeps the solid porous so heat spreads evenly, and also absorbs CO2 (as CaCO3).
Soda lime (CaO + NaOH)a non-deliquescent, easily handled solid base; the reaction is done by heating the dry sodium salt with it.
  • Uses: (1) laboratory preparation of CH4 from CH3COONa and C2H6 from CH3CH2COONa; (2) benzene from sodium benzoate, phenol from sodium salicylate; (3) stepping down a homologous series (one C removed); (4) structure work: the alkane formed shows the carbon skeleton of R in RCOOH.
sodium salicylateNaOH + CaOΔphenol (as phenoxide, then H+)
sodium succinateNaOH + CaO (2 eq)ΔCH3–CH3 (ethane)
sodium terephthalateNaOH + CaOΔbenzene

★ Balanced equations, mechanism and why soda lime instead of NaOH alone

sodium acetate+NaOHCaOΔ, ≈ 300 °CCH₄+Na2CO3
sodium benzoate+NaOHCaOΔbenzene+Na2CO3
sodium propanoate+NaOHCaOΔCH3–CH3 (ethane)+Na2CO3

Usual mechanistic picture: at high temperature the carboxylate loses CO2 to give a carbanion R−; R− takes a proton (from traces of water or from OH−), and the CO2 is trapped by hydroxide as CO32−: CO2 + 2OH− ⟶ CO32− + H2O.

  • Why not NaOH alone? Fused NaOH (m.p. 318 °C) is very corrosive and attacks glass; it also absorbs water from the air (deliquescent) and becomes a sticky liquid. Mixed with CaO it stays a dry, porous solid that can be ground with the salt and heated evenly.
  • Structure and ease: the more stable the carbanion R−, the easier the reaction. Aryl, CCl3− and α-carbonyl carbanions form easily; simple alkyl carbanions need about 300 °C or more.
  • Limitations: good for CH4, C2H6 and arenes; higher acids give lower yields and side products (alkenes, H2, other alkanes), so it is not a general preparation of large alkanes.

4.9 Heating of β,γ-unsaturated and β-keto carboxylic acids

β,γ-Unsaturated acids lose CO2 on simple heating through a six-membered cyclic transition state (no base needed); the double bond shifts.

In general, R–C(=B)–CH2–COOH Δ R–C(BH)=CH2 ⇌ R–C(=B)–CH3

(B = O, N, C)

Mechanism for β-keto acids

Mechanism of the reaction: The decarboxylation of a β-keto acid proceeds through a six-membered cyclic transition state and the process of decarboxylation is promoted by the incipient proton transfer to the keto group through hydrogen bonding. An intermediate enol is formed which rapidly tautomerizes to the more stable keto form. For example, the decarboxylation of 2-ethyl-2-methyl-3-oxobutanoic acid may be shown as follows:

six-membered cyclic transition state (β-keto acid)
enol+CO2tautomeriseketone
2-ethyl-2-methyl-3-oxobutanoic acidΔ, slow−CO2enoltautom.3-methyl-2-pentanone

Evidence for the mechanism: That an enol has been formed as an intermediate can be proved by a trapping experiment. When decarboxylation of the above keto acid is carried out in the presence of bromine (Br2), 3-bromo-3-methyl-2-pentanone is obtained. Since 3-methyl-2-pentanone remains unchanged in the presence of bromine under the condition of decarboxylation as also is the starting β-keto acid, therefore, the isolation of CH3COCBr(CH3)CH2CH3 is a clear evidence for the intermediacy of an enol which forms in the rate-determining step.

enol + Br–Br3-bromo-3-methyl-2-pentanone+ HBr

Another piece of evidence supporting the enol mechanism is that bicyclic β-keto acids, which cannot form enols because strain prevents formation of a double bond at the bridgehead position (Bredt’s rule), are stable towards decarboxylation. For example, the following β-keto acid can be distilled at 310 °C without decomposition.

bicyclic β-keto acid310 °C, −CO2✗enol:double bond at the bridgehead — not formed (sterically not feasible)✗

Decarboxylation of β-keto acids. Decarboxylation requires a carbonyl group two atoms away from the –CO2H. A diacid (R–CH(COOH)–COOH, six-membered cyclic TS) −CO2 an acid enol ⟶ a carboxylic acid. A β-keto acid (R–CO–CH(R)–COOH) −CO2 an enol ⟶ a ketone.

Rule: an acid loses CO2 on heating alone when the carbon two atoms away from the C of COOH carries a C=O, C≡N, NO2, C=C or ring C=N that can accept the electrons (cyclic 6-membered TS → enol / enamine / alkene), or when the carbanion R− is strongly stabilised (CCl3−, polynitroaryl−).

Traps. (i) 3-oxobutanoic acid loses CO2 but 4-oxopentanoic acid (levulinic, a γ-keto acid) does not: the C=O is too far for a 6-membered TS. (ii) A β-keto acid whose enol would put a C=C at a bridgehead (for example ketopinic acid, drawn in the table section below) does not decarboxylate (Bredt's rule). (iii) Benzoic acid needs soda lime; the free acid sublimes unchanged.

★ Red P + HI: conditions, competing reactions and four multifunctional examples

  • Conditions: concentrated HI (57%) with red P, heated under reflux or in a sealed tube (about 150–200 °C for carboxylic acids and alkanes as the target).
  • Function of HI: it is both the acid and the reducing agent. R–OH ⟶ R–I (substitution), then R–I + HI ⟶ R–H + I2. Benzylic and α-carbonyl C–OH groups react most easily.
  • Function of red P: it removes I2 and makes fresh HI (with water), so the reaction is pushed forward and HI is not used up.
  • Mechanism: the R–I ⟶ R–H step is believed to go by attack of I− on the iodine of R–I with protonation of the carbon; the exact path is not settled. [Not verified]
  • Competing reactions: ethers are cleaved (R–O–R′ ⟶ R–I + R′–I); C=C adds HI; carbocation rearrangements can occur; aromatic C–OH and aromatic rings are not reduced.

★ How a metal catalyst works (Horiuti–Polanyi picture)

  • H2 is adsorbed and split into H atoms bound to the metal surface (dissociative adsorption).
  • The alkene lies flat on the surface, bonded through its π electrons.
  • One H atom moves to one carbon: a "half-hydrogenated" alkyl bound to the metal. A second H then gives the alkane, which leaves the surface.
  • Both H atoms come from the surface side, so addition is mainly syn. Because the first step is reversible, the C=C can also move or change geometry (isomerisation), especially on Pd.
FactorEffect on the result
CatalystPd: C=C, C≡C, NO2, benzyl–O hydrogenolysis, can move C=C. Pt/PtO2: also C=O and (in acid, under pressure) benzene rings. Raney Ni: C=C, C=O, C–S. Ni: needs heat and pressure.
Solventacetic acid speeds up PtO2 and helps ring hydrogenation; ethanol and ethyl acetate are common neutral solvents.
Temperature / H2 pressurearene rings need higher pressure or temperature than C=C; harsher conditions also allow hydrogenolysis of strained rings and C–O bonds.
PoisonsS compounds, amines, Pb2+, quinoline, CO bind strongly to the metal. A partly poisoned catalyst is more selective (Lindlar: Pd/CaCO3 + Pb(OAc)2 + quinoline stops at the cis-alkene).

4.13 Hydrogenation with diimide (HN=NH, diazene)

H2N–NH2 (hydrazine) + H–O–O–H Δ H–N=N–H (diimide) + 2H2O

e.g.N2H4H2O2/Δ+ N2↑ + 2H2O

>C=C< + HN=NH ⟶ cyclic TS (both H delivered together from one face: syn) ⟶ H– C–C–H + N2↑

The behavior and reactivity of diimide can be understood best by considering the thermochemistry of hydrogenation of nitrogen:

N≡N + H2 ⟶ HN=NH (diimide) ΔH° = +43.2 kcal; HN=NH + H2 ⟶ H2N–NH2 (hydrazine) ΔH° = −21.6 kcal; H2N–NH2 + H2 ⟶ 2NH3 ΔH° = −43.6 kcal

The first step is strongly endothermic and is the main hurdle to overcome in the hydrogenation of nitrogen to ammonia. Conversely, the reverse reaction, which is the dehydrogenation of diimide, is strongly exothermic. Therefore we may expect that diimide will have a pronounced tendency to revert to molecular nitrogen. This is in fact so and, at normal temperatures, diimide exists only as a transient intermediate that cannot be isolated. It is extremely reactive and readily transfers hydrogen to carbon– carbon multiple bonds:

>C=C< HN=NH –C(H)–C(H)– + N2

–C≡C– HN=NH >C=C< (cis, H and H on the same side) + N2

An important difference between diimide hydrogenation and catalytic hydrogenation is that diimide reacts readily with symmetrical or nonpolar bonds (C=C, C≡C, N=N), whereas hydrogen can add, albeit reluctantly, to polar bonds (C=O, C=N). Diimide does not attack the stronger polar bonds probably because it does not survive long enough to do so. It self-destructs in the absence of a reactive substrate to give nitrogen and hydrazine:

2 HN=NH ⟶ ⟶ N≡N + H2N–NH2

diphenylethyneH2N–NH2+ oxidantcis-stilbene(syn addition of 2H)

★ Making diimide and its mechanism

Way of making HN=NH (in situ)Equation
oxidation of hydrazineH2N–NH2 + H2O2 (Cu2+ cat.) ⟶ HN=NH + 2H2O; or with O2 (air)
potassium azodicarboxylate + acidK+ −O2C–N=N–CO2− K+ + 2CH3COOH ⟶ HN=NH + 2CO2 + 2CH3COOK
tosylhydrazide, heatTsNH–NH2 ⟶(Δ) HN=NH + TsH (sulphinic acid)
cis-diimide + C=C: six-centred TSconcertedsynH–C–C–H (both H on one face) + N≡N
  • The cis form of HN=NH is the one that transfers H; the trans form must isomerise first.
  • Both H atoms move at the same time through a six-membered cyclic TS (a pericyclic group transfer): syn addition. The driving force is the formation of N≡N.
  • Diimide attacks non-polar π bonds (C=C, C≡C, N=N); C=O, C≡N, NO2, C–X, O–O and benzyl–O bonds are left alone (no hydrogenolysis, unlike Pd/H2).
  • Rate: strained > less substituted > more substituted C=C; trans-alkenes faster than cis.

H2, Nicyclohexane only

[Corrected] Cyclobutene + H2/Ni gives cyclobutane as the main product (C=C reduced, ring kept). Butane forms only under the forcing conditions needed to open cyclobutane (≈ 200 °C). But-1-ene and but-2-ene are not formed: they would need the ring C–C bond to break before the C=C is reduced, and C–C hydrogenolysis is far slower than C=C hydrogenation. Cyclopentene and cyclohexene give only the cycloalkane: their rings have little or no strain, so there is no driving force to open them.

★ Hydrogenation or hydrogenolysis? Substituted rings and cyclobutenes

  • Hydrogenation adds H2 across a π bond (C=C). Hydrogenolysis breaks a σ bond (here a ring C–C) with H2. On the same catalyst, C=C hydrogenation is much faster.
  • Why small rings open: cyclopropane and cyclobutane have about 115 and 110 kJ mol−1 strain. Opening releases it, so the reaction is strongly exothermic and the barrier is lower. The bent ("banana") C–C bonds of cyclopropane have p-character and can bind to the metal surface rather like a π bond.
  • Why larger rings resist: cyclopentane (26 kJ mol−1) and cyclohexane (≈ 0) gain little from opening, and their C–C bonds bind poorly to the metal; they open only under forcing conditions on Pt, or not at all.
  • Catalyst: Pt, Pd and Rh open cyclopropanes at lower temperature than Ni.
methylcyclopropaneH₂, PtΔbutane+isobutane
1,1-dimethylcyclopropaneH₂, PtΔneopentane (main)+isopentane

On Pt, the bond between the two least substituted ring carbons (the one farthest from the alkyl groups) is broken most often, because that part of the ring can reach the surface. The ratios depend on metal and temperature. [Not verified]

1-methylcyclobuteneH₂ (1 atm), Pd/C25 °Cmethylcyclobutane (C=C only)
H₂, Ni≈ 200 °Cpentane+isopentane
1,2-dimethylcyclobuteneH₂, Pt25 °Ccis-1,2-dimethylcyclobutane (syn addition)

So for cyclobutene the major product under mild conditions is the cyclobutane; open-chain products need the harsher conditions of cyclobutane hydrogenolysis.

[Corrected] NaBH4 on its own (in water or alcohol) reduces simple alkyl halides only very slowly; it is mainly a reagent for C=O. In a polar aprotic solvent (DMSO) BH4− acts as an SN2 hydride donor, so the order is 1° > 2° and 3° fails. StepEquationComment
Electron transferR–X + Zn ⟶ [R–X]•− + Zn+one electron from the metal surface

RMgX is a very strong base; any compound with an acidic H (more acidic than CH4) gives the alkane. Basicity order: −CH3 > −NH2 > −OH > F−.

★ Numerical problems (volume of gas)

Q1. 0.92 g of ethanol is treated with excess CH3MgI. What volume of CH4 forms at STP (22.4 L mol−1)?

Solution. n(EtOH) = 0.92/46 = 0.02 mol; 1 active H → 0.02 mol CH4 = 448 mL.

Q2. 1.80 g of glucose (C6H12O6) reacts with excess CH3MgI. Volume of CH4 at STP?

Solution. 0.01 mol × 5 OH = 0.05 mol → 1.12 L.

Q3. 0.76 g of a compound C3H8O2 gives 448 mL of CH4 at STP with excess CH3MgI. Suggest structures.

Solution. n = 0.76/76 = 0.01 mol; CH4 = 0.02 mol → 2 active H: a diol, propane-1,2-diol or propane-1,3-diol (not CH3OCH2CH2OH, which has only one).

Q4. 1.38 g of salicylic acid reacts with excess CH3MgBr. Volume of CH4 at 27 °C and 1 atm?

Solution. n = 1.38/138 = 0.01 mol; 2 active H → 0.02 mol; V = nRT/P = 0.02 × 0.0821 × 300 = 0.493 L.

Q5. 0.30 g of an alcohol CnH2n+1OH gives 112 mL of CH4 at STP. Find n.

Solution. mol CH4 = 0.112/22.4 = 0.005 = mol alcohol → M = 0.30/0.005 = 60 → 14n + 18 = 60 → n = 3 (propanol).

Q6. Woulfe bottle. 0.60 g of compound X (one active H) is treated with excess CH3MgI. The CH4 is passed through a Woulfe bottle containing conc. H2SO4 (it absorbs ether vapour and moisture) and is collected over water at 27 °C and 750 mm Hg: volume 259 mL. Aqueous tension at 27 °C = 27 mm Hg. Find the molar mass of X and suggest X.

Solution. p(CH4) = 750 − 27 = 723 mm = 0.951 atm. n = pV/RT = 0.951 × 0.259 / (0.0821 × 300) = 0.0100 mol. One active H → n(X) = 0.0100 mol; M = 0.60/0.0100 = 60 g mol−1: propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol or acetic acid (each has one acidic H). (A Woulfe bottle is a two- or three-necked gas-washing bottle.)

★ More solved examples

Q7. How many litres of CH4 at STP do 0.1 mol of ethanolamine (HOCH2CH2NH2) give with excess CH3MgI on warming?

Solution. OH (1) + NH2 (2) = 3 active H → 0.3 mol = 6.72 L.

Zerewitinoff determination (analysis) counts active H atoms: a weighed sample is treated with excess CH3MgI (in di-n-butyl ether or pyridine) and the CH4 volume is measured. Synthetic use of Grignard reagents is the opposite case: active H must be absent (dry ether, no OH/NH), or the reagent is destroyed before it can add to C=O.

★ More numerical problems

Q8. 0.47 g of phenol reacts with excess CH3MgI. Find the volume of CH4 at 27 °C and 0.821 atm.

Solution. n = 0.47/94 = 0.005 mol CH4. V = nRT/P = 0.005 × 0.0821 × 300/0.821 = 150 mL.

Q9. Limiting reagent. 0.02 mol of ethylene glycol (HOCH2CH2OH) is mixed with 0.03 mol of CH3MgI. Volume of CH4 at STP?

Solution. Active H = 0.04 mol, CH3MgI = 0.03 mol: CH3MgI is limiting. CH4 = 0.03 mol = 672 mL.

Q10. Purity. 2.0 g of impure acetic acid (impurity has no active H) gives 560 mL of CH4 at STP with excess CH3MgI. Find the % purity.

Solution. n(CH4) = 0.025 mol = n(acid); mass = 0.025 × 60 = 1.50 g. Purity = 1.50/2.0 = 75%.

Q11. Mixture. 1.88 g of a mixture of ethanol and phenol gives 672 mL of CH4 at STP with excess CH3MgI. Find the mass of each.

Solution. Let x = mol EtOH, y = mol PhOH: x + y = 0.03; 46x + 94y = 1.88. So 46(0.03 − y) + 94y = 1.88 ⟶ 48y = 0.50 ⟶ y = 0.0104 mol. Phenol = 0.98 g, ethanol = 0.90 g (x = 0.0196 mol).

Q12. Woulfe bottle (hard). 0.177 g of a compound C3H9N is treated with excess CH3MgI in di-n-butyl ether. The gas passes through a Woulfe bottle of conc. H2SO4 (to remove ether vapour and moisture; amine vapour is also held back) and is collected over water at 17 °C and 754 mm Hg: 72.5 mL. Aqueous tension at 17 °C = 14.5 mm Hg. How many active H atoms does the compound have? Suggest its structure.

Solution. p(CH4) = 754 − 14.5 = 739.5 mm = 0.973 atm. n = 0.973 × 0.0725/(0.0821 × 290) = 0.00296 mol. n(compound) = 0.177/59 = 0.0030 mol. Ratio ≈ 1 ⟶ one active H: a 2° amine, ethylmethylamine CH3NHC2H5 (propylamine and isopropylamine have two N–H; trimethylamine has none). Set-up: reaction flask ⟶ Woulfe bottle (inlet tube dipping into the acid, outlet above it) ⟶ gas burette or inverted measuring cylinder over water.

4.17 Frankland reaction

R–X + Zn ⟶ R–Zn–X. The R− of R–Zn–X attacks a second R–X by SN2:

R–Zn–X + R–X SN2 R–R + ZnX2

(overall: R–X + Zn + X–R Δ R–R + ZnX2)

R–Zn–X + R′–X ⟶ R–R′ + ZnX2

It is used to prepare symmetrical and unsymmetrical hydrocarbons.

Step 1 (Zn insertion):  R–X + ZnR–Zn–X (organozinc)
Step 2 (SN2: R− attacks R′–X):  XZn–R  +  CH2–Br–R″R–CH2R″ + ZnXBr
(1)++ ZnClBr
(2)++ ZnCl2
(3)PhCH2–ZnBr ++ ZnBr2
(4)+ PhCH2–Br+ MgBr2

★ What Frankland actually did (verified)

In 1849 Edward Frankland heated ethyl iodide with zinc in a sealed tube. He obtained diethylzinc, the first organometallic compound, and a gas he took to be the free "ethyl radical"; it was later shown to be butane (C2H5–C2H5). [Corrected]

2 C2H5I + 2ZnΔ, sealed tube2 C2H5ZnIΔ(C2H5)2Zn + ZnI2
2 C2H5I + ZnΔC2H5–C2H5 + ZnI2 (coupling)

So "R–X + Zn ⟶ R–R" is correct as an overall equation. The SN2 picture drawn above (R–ZnX attacking R′–X) is a simplification: plain organozinc halides couple with alkyl halides only slowly; modern R–R′ couplings of organozincs need a Pd or Ni catalyst (Negishi coupling). [Not verified]

★ Frankland, Wurtz, Fittig, Wurtz–Fittig, Ullmann compared

ReactionMetal / conditionsHalide(s)ProductMain limitation

Wurtz–FittigNa, dry etherAr–X + R–XAr–R (plus R–R, Ar–Ar)side products

Organozinc halides couple readily with reactive halides (allylic, benzylic) without a catalyst, which is why examples (3) and (4) above work; with plain alkyl halides a Pd or Ni catalyst is normally used (Negishi coupling).

5. Physical Properties of Alkanes

  • Physical state: C1–C4 gases; C5–C17 liquids; C18 onwards solids.
  • Density: density ∝ molar mass. Alkanes are less dense than water.
  • Solubility: like dissolves like — soluble in non-polar solvents, insoluble in water.
  • Melting point: m.p. ∝ close packing, and ∝ molar mass: propane < butane <
hexane. Order of m.p.:<<. Alkanes with an even number of

C atoms generally have a higher m.p. than the adjacent odd alkane — the alternation effect. Among isomers, the more symmetrical one melts higher.

Boiling point: b.p. ∝ molar mass, ∝ surface area. CH4 < CH3–CH3 < CH3CH2CH3. More branching → smaller surface area → lower b.p.:

butane>isobutane;  pentane>isopentane>neopentane

★ 5.1 Boiling and melting points of the pentane isomers

pentane
b.p. 36 °C, m.p. −130 °Cisopentane
b.p. 28 °C, m.p. −160 °Cneopentane

Boiling point falls with branching (smaller surface area, weaker London forces). Melting point of neopentane is highest because the nearly spherical, symmetrical molecule packs best in the crystal.

★ Order questions on b.p. and m.p. (10)

Q1. Increasing b.p.: pentane, isopentane, neopentane.

Solution. neopentane (9.5) < isopentane (27.8) < pentane (36.1 °C). More branching → smaller surface → weaker London forces.

Q2. Increasing b.p.: butane, isobutane.

Solution. isobutane (−11.7) < butane (−0.5 °C).

Q3. Decreasing m.p.: pentane, isopentane, neopentane.

Solution. neopentane (−16.6) > pentane (−129.7) > isopentane (−159.9 °C). The near-spherical neopentane packs best; isopentane (least symmetrical) worst.

Q4. Increasing b.p.: hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,2-dimethylbutane, 2,3-dimethylbutane.

Solution. 2,2-dimethylbutane (49.7) < 2,3-dimethylbutane (58.0) < 2-methylpentane (60.3) < 3-methylpentane (63.3) < hexane (68.7 °C).

Q5. Decreasing m.p. of the hexane isomers.

Solution. hexane (−95) > 2,2-dimethylbutane (−100) > 3-methylpentane (−118) > 2,3-dimethylbutane (−129) > 2-methylpentane (−154 °C).

Q6. Increasing b.p.: pentane, cyclopentane.

Solution. pentane (36.1) < cyclopentane (49.3 °C): the flat, rigid ring has more contact area per molecule.

Q7. Increasing m.p.: pentane, cyclopentane.

Solution. pentane (−129.7) < cyclopentane (−93.9 °C).

Q8. Increasing b.p.: 2,2-dimethylbutane, 2-methylpentane, hexane, heptane.

Solution. 2,2-dimethylbutane (49.7) < 2-methylpentane (60.3) < hexane (68.7) < heptane (98.4 °C).

Q9. Increasing m.p.: methane, ethane, propane, butane.

Solution. propane (−187.7) < ethane (−183.3) < methane (−182.5) < butane (−138.3 °C). Propane, odd and bent, packs worst.

Q10. Increasing b.p.: octane, 2,2,4-trimethylpentane (isooctane), 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane.

Solution. 2,2,4-trimethylpentane (99.2) < 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane (106.5) < octane (125.7 °C).

★ Very hard (5)

Q11. Decreasing m.p.: octane, 2,2,4-trimethylpentane, 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane.

Solution. 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane (+100.7) > octane (−56.8) > 2,2,4-trimethylpentane (−107.4 °C). Symmetry decides m.p.; it does not decide b.p.

Q12. Octane melts 33.8 °C higher than heptane, but nonane melts only 3.3 °C higher than octane. Explain.

Solution. Alternation: going from odd (C7) to even (C8) the packing improves a lot; from even (C8) to odd (C9) the extra CH2 helps but packing gets worse, so the gain is small.

Q13. Arrange by b.p.: neopentane, cyclopentane, pentane, isobutane.

Solution. isobutane (−11.7) < neopentane (9.5) < pentane (36.1) < cyclopentane (49.3 °C).

Q14. Arrange by density: pentane, hexane, cyclohexane, water.

Solution. pentane (0.626) < hexane (0.659) < cyclohexane (0.779) < water (1.00 g mL−1).

Q15. (Z)-but-2-ene boils higher but melts lower than (E)-but-2-ene. Explain both.

Solution. b.p.: Z 3.7 °C > E 0.9 °C, because Z has a small net dipole. m.p.: E −105.5 °C > Z −138.9 °C, because the symmetrical E isomer packs better in the crystal.

★ More solved examples

Q16. Melting points: ethane −183 °C, propane −188 °C, butane −138 °C. Why does propane melt lower than ethane even though it is heavier?

Solution. Alternation: even chains pack better; propane is odd and packs poorly. b.p. shows no such alternation (it depends on the liquid, not the crystal).

Q17. An alkane C5H12 gives only one monochloro product. Identify it and its b.p. rank among the isomers.

Solution. Neopentane, C(CH3)4: lowest b.p. of the three (9.5 °C).

Q18. Hexane has density 0.659 g mL−1 but cyclohexane 0.779; hexane melts at −95 °C but cyclohexane at +6.5 °C. Explain.

Solution. The compact, rigid ring packs closely (higher density) and fits well into a crystal; the floppy chain does not.

Q19. 2,2,3,3-Tetramethylbutane boils at 106.5 °C but melts at 100.7 °C. Why is it a liquid over only ~6 °C?

Solution. Almost spherical: small surface → low b.p.; very symmetrical → very high m.p. So m.p. and b.p. nearly meet (it sublimes easily).

Q20. Propane (M 44), dimethyl ether (M 46) and ethanol (M 46) boil at −42, −24 and 78 °C. Explain.

Solution. London forces only; plus a dipole; plus O–H···O hydrogen bonds.

Q21. Why do alkanes not dissolve in water even though mixing is nearly thermoneutral?

Solution. Water around the alkane becomes ordered (cage-like), so ΔS is strongly negative and ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is positive (hydrophobic effect).

★ What decides b.p. and m.p.

All b.p. values are normal boiling points (at 1 atm = 101.3 kPa); m.p. values are at 1 atm. Data: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics.

FactorEffect on b.p.Effect on m.p.
Molar mass (chain length)rises steadily (more London forces)rises, but zig-zags: even chains pack better (alternation)
Branchinglowers b.p. (less surface contact)irregular: high symmetry (neopentane, 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane) raises m.p. sharply
Symmetry / shapesmall effectlarge effect: compact symmetrical molecules pack well
Ring vs chaincycloalkane boils higher (rigid, more contact)cycloalkane usually melts higher
cis / trans (alkenes)cis often higher (small dipole)trans higher (packs better)

Reliable trends: b.p. rises with chain length and falls with branching for isomers. Special cases: m.p. depends on crystal packing, so it does not follow branching; highly symmetrical molecules can melt close to (or even above) their boiling point and may sublime.

★ 5.2 Conformations of butane (energy vs dihedral angle)

★ Solved examples on conformations

Q1. In butane the gauche form is 3.8 kJ mol−1 above anti. Calculate the % of anti at 25 °C.

Solution. K = [gauche]/[anti] = 2 e−3800/(8.314 × 298) = 0.431 → % anti = 1/1.431 = 70%.

Q2. For methylcyclohexane the axial form is 7.3 kJ mol−1 less stable. % equatorial at 25 °C?

Solution. K = e7300/2478 = 19 → 95% equatorial.

Q3. Estimate the rate of rotation about C–C in ethane at 25 °C (barrier 12 kJ mol−1; kBT/h = 6.2 × 1012 s−1).

Solution. k = 6.2 × 1012 × e−12000/2478 ≈ 5 × 1010 s−1.

Q4. Staggered conformers of 2,3-dimethylbutane about C2–C3: which is most stable?

Solution. H anti to H: 2 gauche CH3/CH3; H gauche to H (two mirror forms): 3 gauche. The H-anti form is more stable by about 3.8 kJ mol−1.

Q5. Most stable conformation of cis-1-t-butyl-4-methylcyclohexane?

Solution. t-Butyl equatorial (axial costs ≈ 20 kJ), so the methyl is axial: the ring is locked.

Q6. Why is anti-1,2-dichloroethane more favoured in the gas phase than in a polar solvent?

Solution. Anti has no dipole; gauche has one. A polar solvent stabilises the polar gauche form.

★ 5.3 Heats of combustion and stability of isomers

Isomer (C8H18)−ΔHc / kJ mol−1
octane5471
2-methylheptane5466
2,2-dimethylhexane5458
2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane5452

Isomers give the same products (8CO2 + 9H2O), so a smaller heat of combustion means a more stable (lower-energy) isomer: more branched alkanes are more stable. Between homologues, −ΔHc rises by about 658 kJ mol−1 per CH2.

★ 10 hard questions on the order of heats of combustion

Rule: for isomers (same products), the less stable isomer gives more heat. Strain (angle, torsional, steric) raises the heat of combustion.

Q1. Increasing −ΔHc per CH2: cyclopropane, cyclobutane, cyclopentane, cyclohexane.

Solution. cyclohexane (658.6) < cyclopentane (664.0) < cyclobutane (686.2) < cyclopropane (697.1 kJ mol−1). Strain: 0 < 26 < 110 < 115 kJ.

Q2. Increasing −ΔHc of the C6H12 isomers cyclohexane, methylcyclopentane, hex-1-ene.

Solution. cyclohexane < methylcyclopentane < hex-1-ene (ΔHf(g) ≈ −123, −106, −42 kJ mol−1). The strain-free chair is the most stable; a C=C is less stable than a ring C–C.

Q3. Which gives more heat: cis- or trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane?

Solution. cis (one CH3 must be axial: a/e) is less stable than trans (e/e) by ≈ 7 kJ, so cis has the larger −ΔHc.

Q4. cis- or trans-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane?

Solution. trans (a/e) is less stable than cis (e/e), so trans gives more heat.

Q5. cis- or trans-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane?

Solution. cis (a/e) gives more heat; trans can be e/e.

Q6. Increasing energy (and so −ΔHc, if each conformer could be burnt frozen) of cyclohexane conformers: chair, boat, twist-boat, half-chair.

Solution. chair (0) < twist-boat (≈ 23) < boat (≈ 29) < half-chair (≈ 45 kJ mol−1). The half-chair is the transition state between chair and twist-boat.

Q7. Planar cyclopentane vs the real envelope form: which would give more heat, and why does cyclopentane pucker?

Solution. Planar: angle 108° (almost no angle strain) but all 10 C–H pairs eclipsed (≈ 40 kJ torsional strain). The envelope (one C out of plane) relieves much of this, so its strain is only ≈ 26 kJ. The planar form would give more heat.

Q8. Axial- vs equatorial-methylcyclohexane: which conformer has the higher energy content?

Solution. Axial, by ≈ 7.3 kJ mol−1 (two 1,3-diaxial CH3/H interactions = like two gauche butane units).

Q9. Increasing −ΔHc: pentane, isopentane, neopentane.

Solution. neopentane < isopentane < pentane (ΔHf(g) ≈ −168, −154, −147 kJ mol−1). More branching → more stable.

Q10. cis- or trans-decalin: which gives more heat on combustion?

Solution. cis-decalin (one ring bond axial to the other ring; ≈ 11 kJ mol−1 less stable than all-equatorial trans).

Q11. Increasing −ΔHc of the butenes: but-1-ene, (Z)-but-2-ene, (E)-but-2-ene, 2-methylpropene.

Solution. 2-methylpropene < (E)-but-2-ene < (Z)-but-2-ene < but-1-ene (more substituted, less crowded C=C is more stable).

★ More solved examples

Q12. Total ring strain from heats of combustion per CH2 (unstrained value 658.6 kJ): cyclopropane 697.1, cyclobutane 686.2.

Solution. (697.1 − 658.6) × 3 = 115 kJ; (686.2 − 658.6) × 4 = 110 kJ.

Q13. Among the C8H18 isomers in the table, which has the lowest heat of combustion?

Solution. 2,2,3,3-Tetramethylbutane (5452 kJ mol−1): the most branched, most stable.

★ Sign of ΔHc and when a comparison is fair

  • ΔHc is negative (heat is given out). "Larger heat of combustion" means a larger magnitude |ΔHc|, i.e. a more negative ΔHc. In these notes the tables list −ΔHc (a positive number) to avoid confusion.
  • Stability can be read from heats of combustion only for isomers (same formula, so the same CO2 and H2O are formed). For different formulae, normalise first: per CH2 group for cycloalkanes, or compare ΔHf instead.
  • Conformers (chair vs boat, axial vs equatorial) interconvert quickly, so they cannot be burned separately; their "heat of combustion" difference is the energy difference between them (from calculation or equilibrium data).

6. Chemical Reactions of Alkanes

6.1 Free-radical substitution — halogenation

CH4 + X2 hν CH3–X + HX

A chain reaction mechanism explains the chlorination of methane. A chain reaction has three kinds of steps:

1. Initiation — generates a reactive intermediate: X2 hν X• + X•

2. Propagation — the reactive intermediate reacts with a stable molecule to form a product and another reactive intermediate, so the chain continues until the reactants are used up or the intermediate is destroyed: X• + H–CH3 RDS HX + •CH3 (planar) •CH3 + X–X ⟶ CH3X + X•

3. Termination — side reactions that destroy reactive intermediates and slow or stop the reaction: X• + X• ⟶ X2; R• + R• ⟶ R–R; R• + X• ⟶ R–X

  • Chain reaction; free-radical intermediate.
  • Formation of •CH3 (R•) is the RDS, so a kinetic isotope effect is present (C–H is broken in the RDS).
  • Order of reaction rate: 3° > 2° > 1° H. Order of reactivity of X2: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.
  • The reaction is slowed by radical scavengers (inhibitors) such as O2: X• + •O–O• ⟶ X–O–O• (a much less reactive radical).

Fluorination

Highly explosive; also forms carbon black: CH4 + 2F2 ⟶ C + 4HF (redox).

Very early T.S. (R···H···F) with mainly F• character, so the T.S. is independent of R• stability and Ea is about the same for 1°, 2°, 3° H: fluorination is unselective.

CH3CH2CH3 + F2 ⟶ 1° H abstraction (CH3CH2CH2•) or 2° H abstraction ((CH3)2CH•)

Per-H selectivity of fluorination: 1° H : 2° H : 3° H = 1 : 1 : 1.

the second (Ea = 4, ΔH° = −110) is fast; overall ΔH° = −105 kJ/mol.

Tertiary radical formation is more exothermic, yet more primary alkyl chloride forms. Once the 9 : 1 ratio of primary to tertiary H atoms is taken into account:

tertiary : primary
ratio of products37 : 63
number of H atoms1 : 9
relative reactivity of each C–H37/1 : 63/9 = 37 : 7 ≈ 5 : 1

The rate of attack by Cl• on a tertiary C–H bond, then, is about five times the rate of attack by Cl• on a primary C–H bond. We said that this is because the formation of the tertiary radical is more exothermic than the formation of the primary radical. But the rate of a reaction depends not on ΔH for that reaction but on the activation energy of the reaction; in other words, the energy needed to reach the transition state for the reaction. But we can still use the stability of the product radicals as a guide to the stability of the transition state because the transition state must have significant radical character.

The energy diagram above illustrates this point. As the reactants (Cl• plus isobutane) move towards the products, they pass through a transition state (TS1 for formation of the primary radical, TS3 for formation of the tertiary) in which the radical character of the Cl• starting material is spread over both the Cl and the C centres. The greater stability of a tertiary radical compared with a primary one must be reflected to a lesser degree in these transition states: a radical shared between Cl and a tertiary centre will be more stable than a radical shared between Cl and a primary centre. The transition state TS3 for the reaction at the tertiary C–H bond is therefore of lower energy than the transition state TS1 for the reaction at the primary C–H bond. In other words, the activation energy ΔG3‡ is smaller than ΔG1‡, so reaction at the tertiary C–H bond is faster.

Bromination

The first step (H-abstraction by Br•) is endothermic for both 1° and 3° H, but more so for the 1° radical, so the 3° radical is strongly preferred. CH4 + Br2 ⟶ CH3Br + HBr.

Chlorination is fast but less selective; bromination is slow but more selective. Relative reactivity per H towards bromination: 1° H : 2° H : 3° H = 1 : 82 : 1600.

Example. Calculate the enthalpy of each step in the bromination of ethane and the overall enthalpy (bond energies in kcal/mol).

Initiation: Br–Br ⟶ 2Br• Propagation 1: Br• + CH3CH3 ⟶ H–Br + CH3CH2•: break H–C (+100.5), form H–Br (−87) ⟹ +13.5. Propagation 2: CH3CH2• + Br–Br ⟶ CH3CH2Br + Br•: break Br–Br (+45), form C–Br (−70) ⟹ −25. Total = −11.5 kcal/mol.

The enthalpy of reaction is the sum of the propagation steps (−11.5 kcal/mol). The first step is endothermic (+13.5 kcal); this is the lower limit of Ea for that step (Ea = 14.0 ± 0.25 kcal/mol has been reported).

Why is bromination much more selective than chlorination? (Hammond postulate)

In bromination the products of the first step (R• + HBr) are higher in energy than the reactants, so the T.S. is late and resembles the radical being formed. The energy difference between 1° and 3° radicals is therefore strongly reflected in TS1 and TS3: ΔG1‡ ≫ ΔG3‡.

This is a good example of the Hammond postulate, applied to real chemistry. Because the products of the first step (R• plus HBr) are higher in energy than the starting materials, the transition state must be similar in structure and energy to the radical being formed: the difference in energies of the primary and tertiary product radicals should therefore be markedly reflected in the different energies of the transition states TS1 and TS3, and ΔG1‡ will be significantly larger than ΔG3‡. For the chlorination reaction, the products were just slightly lower in energy than the starting materials, so the transition states for the two possible reactions both resembled the starting materials rather more and the products rather less. These are the same for both tertiary and primary hydrogen abstractions, of course, so the difference in energy of the product radicals exerts a less pronounced effect on the difference in energy of the transition states.

Iodination

Radical iodination is impossible because the final step is insufficiently exothermic to make up for the endothermic formation of the alkyl radical. It is highly reversible in nature: RH + I2 ⇌ R–I + HI, and HI is a strong reducing agent. Iodination is carried out in the presence of oxidising agents e.g. HNO3, PbO2 etc.: HI HNO3 I2.
