★ 6.2 Free-radical halogenation in depth: energetics, Hammond postulate and Eₐ of 1°, 2°, 3° H

This section builds on 6.1 (mechanism, % yield method), 6.15–6.17 (counting products, 2-methylbutane, ΔH of each step). It does not repeat them; it adds the energy profiles for every halogen, the Hammond postulate in numbers, the activation energies of 1°, 2° and 3° H, and how selectivity changes with temperature.

(a) The chain, step by step

Step 1 decides which H is replaced (it fixes the radical, so it fixes the product) and is the slow step for Cl, Br and I. The X• made in step 2 starts step 1 again, so one photon can give thousands of product molecules (a long chain). The overall ΔH is the sum of step 1 and step 2 only; initiation and termination are too rare to count.

(b) Energy profile for each halogen (CH₄ + X₂; kJ mol⁻¹; step-2 barriers are small and drawn schematically)

  • F: step 1 is strongly exothermic, Eₐ ≈ 5 kJ. Even in the dark F₂ reacts, because F₂ + CH₄ ⟶ •CH₃ + HF + F• is only about +27 kJ (439 + 158 − 570), so the chain starts without light. Too fast to control; C–C bonds also break.
  • Cl: step 1 slightly endothermic (+7), Eₐ = 17; step 2 is very exothermic (−111) and pulls the reaction. Needs light or heat to start, then fast.
  • Br: step 1 strongly endothermic (+73), Eₐ = 75. Slow, so only the weakest C–H bonds (3°, allylic, benzylic) react at a useful rate.
  • I: step 1 is +141, so Eₐ ≥ 141 kJ. The chain cannot keep going at normal temperature, and the overall reaction is endothermic (+54). HI also reduces R–I back to R–H.

(c) Bell–Evans–Polanyi plot: Eₐ against ΔH of step 1

The more endothermic the step, the higher Eₐ. For an endothermic step Eₐ can never be smaller than ΔH, so Br and I sit almost on the line Eₐ = ΔH: their transition states are almost the products. For F and Cl, Eₐ is far above ΔH (and above zero), so the TS is reached early, long before the H is transferred.

(d) The Hammond postulate

Statement: a transition state looks most like (in structure and energy) the species nearest to it in energy. So for a fast, exothermic step the TS is early and looks like the reactants; for a slow, endothermic step the TS is late and looks like the products.

Chlorination TS [R···H···Cl]‡Bromination TS [R···H···Br]‡
C–H bond in the TSonly slightly stretchedalmost broken
H–X bond in the TShardly formedalmost formed
Radical character on carbonsmalllarge (looks like R•)
Does the TS "feel" the stability of R•?only a littlealmost fully
Resultsmall ΔEₐ between 1°, 2°, 3° H → low selectivitylarge ΔEₐ → high selectivity

(e) Eₐ and reactivity of 1°, 2° and 3° H

Weaker C–H bonds give more stable radicals. Bond dissociation energies (modern gas-phase values, Blanksby & Ellison, Acc. Chem. Res. 2003):

The more reactive the radical, the less it can tell different C–H bonds apart. This is a useful rule, not a law: it works well inside one family such as the halogen atoms.

(h) Kinetics of the chain (steady-state approximation)

Photochemical initiation: Cl₂ + hν ⟶ 2Cl• (rate = 2φIabs). Propagation: Cl• + RH ⟶ R• + HCl (kp1); R• + Cl₂ ⟶ RCl + Cl• (kp2). Termination: 2Cl• ⟶ Cl₂ (kt). In the steady state, radicals are made as fast as they are destroyed: 2φIabs = 2kt[Cl•]2, so [Cl•] = (φIabs/kt)1/2 and

rate = kp1[RH](φIabs/kt)1/2

  • Rate ∝ (light intensity)1/2: four times the light gives only twice the rate (more radicals also means more termination).
  • Chain length = rate of propagation / rate of initiation = kp1[RH]/(φIabskt)1/2: it is longer at low light intensity.
  • Thermal initiation (Cl₂ ⟶ 2Cl•, ki) gives rate = kp1(ki/kt)1/2[RH][Cl₂]1/2, i.e. half order in Cl₂.

(i) Evidence that step 1 is H-abstraction (not X-abstraction)

  • The alternative step 1, X• + CH₄ ⟶ CH₃X + H•, would need to make a free H• (H–C 439 broken, C–Cl 351 made: +88 kJ for Cl). That is far worse than +7, so it is not used.
  • Kinetic isotope effect: C–H reacts faster than C–D, so the C–H bond breaks in the slow step. The effect is smaller for Cl• (early TS, C–H only slightly stretched) than for Br• (late TS, C–H nearly broken). [Trend only; exact numbers vary.]
  • Traces of ethane are found in the chlorination of methane: 2•CH₃ ⟶ C₂H₆ (termination).
  • O₂ (a diradical) causes an induction period, and the reaction stops in the dark: both point to a radical chain.

(j) Polar and solvent effects (beyond the simple 1 : 3.8 : 5 rule)

  • Cl• is an electrophilic radical. In the TS a little positive charge builds up on carbon ([Rδ+···H···Clδ−]‡), so an electron-withdrawing group nearby slows attack on its own and the next carbon. In 1-chlorobutane the C-1 and C-2 hydrogens are deactivated and C-3 is attacked most (see 6.20, Q4).
  • Solvent: in benzene, Cl• forms a weak π-complex with the ring; this complexed Cl• is less reactive and therefore more selective. For 2,3-dimethylbutane the 3° : 1° per-H ratio rises from about 4 in the neat alkane to several tens in concentrated benzene (G. A. Russell, 1958). [Order of magnitude only.]
  • Stereochemistry: the alkyl radical is planar (or a fast-inverting shallow pyramid), so a stereocentre that becomes the radical carbon gives a racemic product (see 6.10).

★ 10 hard questions: total monochloro isomers with the existing groups kept in place

Count constitutional isomers first, then add stereoisomers. The orientation (cis/trans) of the groups already present does not change, because the reaction does not touch those carbons. Achiral starting material → both enantiomers of a chiral product form. All counts below were checked by computer enumeration of every H replaced by Cl.

Q1. Total number of monochloro derivatives (including stereoisomers) of cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane, keeping the original orientation of the existing alkyl groups.

Solution. 4 constitutional, 12 in total. CH2Cl (2: chiral, both enantiomers); C-1 (2); C-3 = C-6 (2 diastereomers × 2 = 4); C-4 = C-5 (4).

Q2. Total number of monochloro derivatives (including stereoisomers) of trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane (racemic), keeping the original orientation of the existing alkyl groups.

Solution. 4 constitutional, 12 in total. same four positions; each enantiomer of the starting material gives its own products.

Q3. Total number of monochloro derivatives (including stereoisomers) of cis-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane, keeping the original orientation of the existing alkyl groups.

Solution. 5 constitutional, 12 in total. CH2Cl (2); C-1 (2); C-2 (2, both achiral: Cl cis or trans to the CH3 groups); C-4 = C-6 (4); C-5 (2, achiral).

Q4. Total number of monochloro derivatives (including stereoisomers) of cis-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane, keeping the original orientation of the existing alkyl groups.

Solution. 3 constitutional, 6 in total. CH2Cl (1); C-1 (1); C-2 (2 diastereomers, each chiral → 4).

Q5. Total number of monochloro derivatives (including stereoisomers) of trans-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane, keeping the original orientation of the existing alkyl groups.

Solution. 3 constitutional, 6 in total. CH2Cl (1); C-1 (1); C-2 (4).

Q6. Total number of monochloro derivatives (including stereoisomers) of cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane, keeping the original orientation of the existing alkyl groups.

Solution. 3 constitutional, 6 in total. CH2Cl (2); C-1 (2); C-3 (2: Cl syn or anti to the CH3 groups, both achiral).

Q7. Total number of monochloro derivatives (including stereoisomers) of trans-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane (racemic), keeping the original orientation of the existing alkyl groups.

Solution. 3 constitutional, 6 in total. CH2Cl (2); C-1 (2); C-3 (2: the two faces are the same by the C2 axis, so one product per enantiomer).

Q8. Total number of monochloro derivatives (including stereoisomers) of cis-1,3-dimethylcyclobutane, keeping the original orientation of the existing alkyl groups.

Solution. 3 constitutional, 4 in total. CH2Cl (1); C-1 (1); C-2 (2, both achiral).

Q9. Total number of monochloro derivatives (including stereoisomers) of cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopentane, keeping the original orientation of the existing alkyl groups.

Solution. 4 constitutional, 10 in total. CH2Cl (2); C-1 (2); C-3 (4); C-4 (2).

Q10. Total number of monochloro derivatives (including stereoisomers) of ethylcyclohexane, keeping the original orientation of the existing alkyl groups.

Solution. 6 constitutional, 14 in total. CH2CH2Cl (1); CHCl (2); C-1 (1); C-2 (4); C-3 (4); C-4 (2: cis/trans).

6.6 Radical inhibitors

We often want to prevent or retard free-radical reactions. For example, oxygen in the air oxidises and spoils foods, solvents, and other compounds mostly by free-radical chain reactions. Chemical intermediates may decompose or polymerise by free-radical chain reactions. Even the cells in living systems are damaged by radical reactions, which can lead to aging, cancerous mutations, or cell death.

Radical inhibitors are often added to foods and chemicals to retard spoilage by radical chain reactions. Chain reactions depend on the individual steps being fast, so that each initiation step results in many molecules reacting, as in the reaction-energy diagram at the left in Figure 4-13. (Only the radicals are shown.) The diagram at right in the figure shows how an inhibitor (I) can stop the chain by reacting with a radical intermediate in a fast, highly exothermic step to form an intermediate that is relatively stable. The next step in the chain becomes endothermic and very slow.

Side note: A radical chain reaction must be a series of exothermic (or mildly endothermic) steps because each step must go quickly, before a termination reaction occurs. An inhibitor reacts with a radical to give a relatively stable product that ends the chain, because it would require a strongly endothermic step for the chain reaction to continue.

add I

“Butylated hydroxyanisole” (BHA) is often added to foods as an antioxidant. It stops oxidation by reacting with radical intermediates to form a relatively stable free-radical intermediate (BHA radical). The BHA radical can react with a second free radical to form an even more stable quinone with all its electrons paired.

RO• or R• +BHAROH or RH +BHA radical (stabilised)
RO• or R•ROCH3 or RCH3 +quinone (all electrons paired)

Radical inhibitors also help to protect the cells of living systems. Like BHA, vitamin E is a phenol (an aromatic ring with an –OH group), and it is thought to react with radicals by losing the OH hydrogen atom as just shown for BHA. Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is also thought to protect cells from free radicals, possibly by the following mechanism:

RO• +ascorbic acidROH +

Application — cancer drugs. Some anti-cancer agents act by generating highly reactive hydroxyl radicals, which damage the DNA of rapidly dividing tumour cells, so the tumour shrinks. Example: bleomycin (used for testicular cancer).

6.7 Free-radical addition of HBr to alkenes and alkynes (anti-Markovnikov rule, peroxide effect, Kharasch effect)

When the negative part of an unsymmetrical reagent adds to an unsymmetrical alkene in the presence of sunlight or peroxide, it goes to the carbon that bears the greater number of hydrogens: RCH=CH2 + HX R2O2hν RCH2–CH2–X. Among hydrogen halides, only HBr follows the anti-Markovnikov rule.

THE MECHANISM — (a) Initiation. Step 1: The weak O–O bond of the peroxide undergoes homolytic dissociation to give two alkoxy radicals: RO–OR light or heat 2RO•

Step 2: An alkoxy radical abstracts a hydrogen atom from hydrogen bromide, generating a bromine atom and setting the stage for a chain reaction: RO• + H–Br ⟶ RO–H (alcohol) + Br• (bromine atom)

(b) Chain propagation. Step 3: The regiochemistry of addition is set in this step. Bromine bonds to C-1 of 1-butene to give a secondary radical (1-(bromomethyl)propyl radical). If it had bonded to C-2, a less stable primary radical would have resulted.

Step 4: The radical produced in step 3 abstracts a hydrogen atom from hydrogen bromide giving the product 1-bromobutane. This hydrogen abstraction also generates a bromine atom, which reacts with another molecule of alkene as in step 3. Steps 3 and 4 repeat many times unless interrupted by chain termination steps. (Propagation, general form: P-1 X• adds to the CH2 end; P-2 the radical abstracts H from HX.)

Termination: RO• + RO• ⟶ R2O2; X• + X• ⟶ X2

Bond energies (kJ/mol): C=C π-bond 270; H–F 570; C–F 485; C–H 410; H–Cl 431; C– Cl 330; C–Br 285; H–Br 366; C–I 240; H–I 297.

XP-1: CH3CH=CH2 + X• → CH3C•HCH2XP-2: CH3C•HCH2X + HX → CH3CH2CH2X + X•
FΔH = 270 − 485 = −215 (exo)ΔH = 570 − 410 = +160 (endo)
ClΔH = 270 − 330 = −60 (exo)ΔH = 431 − 410 = +21 (endo)
BrΔH = 270 − 285 = −15 (exo)ΔH = 366 − 410 = −44 (exo)
IΔH = 270 − 240 = +30 (endo)ΔH = 297 − 410 = −113 (exo)

6.8 Metal–ammonia reduction of alkynes (Birch-type)

3-hexyneNaNH3 (l)trans-3-hexene (82%)

THE OVERALL REACTION. On dissolving in liquid ammonia, sodium atoms dissociate into sodium ions and electrons, both of which are solvated by ammonia. To reflect this, the solvated electrons are represented in the equation as e−(am).

RC≡CR′ + 2e−(am) + 2NH3 ⟶ (E)-RCH=CHR′ + 2NH2− (alkyne + electrons + ammonia ⟶ (E)-alkene + amide ion)

THE MECHANISM.

Step 1: Electron transfer. An electron adds to one of the triply bonded carbons to give an anion radical: RC≡CR′ + e−(am) ⇌fast RC•=C−R′ (anion radical).

Step 2: Proton transfer. The anion radical formed in the first step is strongly basic and abstracts a proton from ammonia. This is believed to be the rate-determining step. The alkenyl radical that results is a mixture of rapidly equilibrating E and Z stereoisomers: RC•=C−R′ + H–NH2 slow RC•=CHR′ (alkenyl radical, E/Z mixture) + −NH2 (amide ion).

Step 3: Electron transfer. The alkenyl radical reacts with a solvated electron to give a vinyl anion. The more stable E-alkenyl anion predominates and E–Z equilibration is slow: RC•=CHR′ + e−(am) fast RC−=CHR′ (alkenyl anion, mainly E).

Step 4: Proton transfer. The alkenyl anion abstracts a proton from ammonia to form the alkene. The E/Z ratio of the product reflects the E/Z ratio of the alkenyl anion: H2N–H + RC−=CHR′ fast RCH=CHR′ (alkene, mainly E) + −NH2 (amide ion).

Q. Tertiary H atoms react with Cl• about 5.5 times as fast as primary ones. Predict the product ratio for chlorination of isobutane.

Solution. Isobutane has 9 primary H and 1 tertiary H. (9 × 1.0) = 9.0; (1 × 5.5) = 5.5. Even though the primary hydrogens are less reactive, there are so many of them that the primary product is the major product. The product ratio will be 9.0 : 5.5, or about 1.6 : 1. Fraction primary = 9.0/14.5 = 62% ((CH3)2CHCH2Cl, major); fraction tertiary = 5.5/14.5 = 38% ((CH3)3CCl, minor).

6.11 Nitration

When nitration is carried out in the vapour phase between 420 K and 720 K, a mixture of all possible mono-nitro derivatives is obtained (C–C bonds also break).

CH3CH2CH3 + HNO3 450 °C 1-nitropropane 25% + 2-nitropropane 40% + nitroethane 10% + nitromethane 25%

Mechanism (free-radical substitution).

  • Step I: HO–NO2 Δ HO• + •NO2
  • R–H + •OH ⟶ R• + H2O. Step II: R• + HO–NO2 ⟶ R–NO2 (product) + •OH. Step III (termination): R• + •NO2 ⟶ R–NO2
  • R• + •OH ⟶ R–OH (minor)
  • •OH + •NO2 ⟶ HONO2

6.12 Sulphonation

Replacement of an H atom of an alkane by –SO3H is sulphonation. Alkanes react with fuming H2SO4 or oleum (H2S2O7); branched lower alkanes and higher alkanes give alkanesulphonic acids. Lower members (propane, butane, pentane) react with SO3 in the vapour phase: C3H8 + SO3 ⟶ C3H7–SO3H.

(CH3)3C–H + H2SO4 (oleum) ⟶ (CH3)3C–SO3H + H2O

Reactivity order: 3° H > 2° H > 1° H

Mechanism (free-radical substitution, as given in the source): [Not verified] I could not confirm this HO•/•SO3H scheme in standard texts; treat it as a coaching-note mechanism.

  • HO–SO3H 400 °C HO• + •SO3H
  • RH + •OH ⟶ R• + H2O (e.g. C6H13H ⟶ C6H13•)
  • R• + •SO3H ⟶ R–SO3H

6.14 Isomerisation

Alkanes on heating with anhydrous AlCl3 (+ HCl) isomerise to branched alkanes.AlCl3Δ

Mechanism (carbocation, not radical): AlCl3 (with a trace of HCl) abstracts a hydride from a 2° C–H: CH3CH2CH2CH3 + AlCl3 Δ CH3–C+H–CH2CH3 + H– AlCl3−. The cation rearranges (methyl shift, reversible): CH3–C+H–CH2CH3 ⇌ (CH3)2CH–C+H2 ⇌ (CH3)3C+ (after a 1,2-H shift, the 3° cation). H–AlCl3− then returns the hydride, giving isobutane + AlCl3 (the more stable branched isomer).

6.16 Cracking of hydrocarbons (pyrolysis)

A process in which high-boiling hydrocarbons are converted into low-boiling hydrocarbons by heat. Cracking involves breaking of C–H and C–C bonds (free-radical mechanism). C6H14 773 K C6H12 + H2, or C4H8 + C2H6, or C3H6 + C2H4 + CH4

C12H26 PtPd/Ni/973 K C7H16 + C5H10 + other products

Mechanism (butane, 400–500 °C):

  • CH3–CH2CH2CH3 ⟶ •CH3 + •CH2CH2CH3 ⟶ (disproportionation) CH4 + CH2=CHCH3
  • CH3CH2–CH2CH3 ⟶ 2CH3CH2• ⟶ CH3CH3 + CH2=CH2

Read also: knocking, octane number and cetane number.

6.17 Reed reaction (sulphochlorination)

[Corrected] The Reed reaction uses SO2 and Cl2 together in light and gives an alkanesulphonyl chloride: RH + SO2 + Cl2 hν R–SO2Cl + HCl. (The old text gave RCl here; that is a different reaction, shown below.)

Chain: Cl2 hν 2Cl•; RH + Cl• ⟶ R• + HCl; R• + SO2 ⟶ R–SO2•; R–SO2• + Cl2 ⟶ R–SO2Cl + Cl•. Example: C6H12 (cyclohexane) + SO2 + Cl2 ⟶ cyclohexanesulphonyl chloride + HCl.

Chlorination with sulphuryl chloride (Kharasch–Brown): RH + SO2Cl2 (PhCO2)2 or hν R–Cl + SO2 + HCl. Chain: R• + SO2Cl2 ⟶ R–Cl + •SO2Cl; •SO2Cl ⟶ SO2 + Cl•; Cl• + RH ⟶ HCl + R•.

6.18 NBS and NCS — allylic and benzylic halogenation

NBS = N-bromosuccinimide;   NCS = N-chlorosuccinimide

Preparation of NBS

succinic acidNH32 eqammonium succinateΔ−2H2O
succinamideΔ−NH3succinimideKOH−H2OBr–BrNBS

Properties

  • NBS is an oxidising agent. It oxidises allylic and benzylic positions by substituting H by Br.
  • It can also oxidise 1° and 2° alcohols to aldehydes and ketones: RCH2OH NBS RCHO; RCH(OH)R NBS R–CO–R
  • Pure NBS is inert. NBS first reacts with a trace of HBr to liberate a small amount of Br2, which gives Br•; Br• forms R• and HBr, which reacts again with NBS to give Br2. So NBS supplies Br2 continuously in small instalments.
  • NBS keeps the concentration of Br2 low during allylic bromination. If Br2 is in excess, addition to C=C as well as radical bromination takes place.
  • The RDS of radical addition (Br• + C=C) is reversible, while the RDS of allylic substitution is irreversible. At low [Br2] the addition goes backwards and allylic substitution gives the major product.
  • If direct bromination of an alkene is done at 400–500 °C, addition does not occur and allylic substitution takes place: addition is favoured by enthalpy but opposed by entropy (ΔH = −ve, ΔS = −ve), so ΔG = +ve for addition at high temperature.
Br2500 °C  NBSCCl4, hν  PhCH3NBSCCl4, hνPhCH2–Br

★ 6.19 Solved examples on alkane reactions

Q1. Calculate the % of each product in the monochlorination of butane (1° : 2° = 1 : 3.8).

Solution. 1° H: 6 × 1 = 6; 2° H: 4 × 3.8 = 15.2; total 21.2. 1-chlorobutane = 28%, 2-chlorobutane = 72% (racemic).

Q2. Which alkane C6H14 gives only two monochloro isomers?

Solution. 2,3-Dimethylbutane (12 equivalent 1° H and 2 equivalent 3° H).

Q3. Light-induced chlorination of (S)-2-chlorobutane gives 2,3-dichlorobutane. Is it optically active?

Solution. The radical forms at C-3 while C-2 keeps its configuration, so two diastereomers form: meso-2,3-dichlorobutane (inactive) and (2S,3S)-2,3-dichlorobutane (active). The mixture is optically active.

Q4. A mixture of CH4 and Cl2 is kept in the dark at room temperature. Does it react? What if it is first irradiated and then kept in the dark?

Solution. In the dark no Cl• forms, so no reaction. Once started by light, the chain continues for only a very short time in the dark, because radicals are destroyed by termination within fractions of a second.

Q5. Why does adding a little O2 stop the chlorination of methane for a while (induction period)?

Solution. O2 is a diradical; it traps •CH3 as CH3OO•, which is too unreactive to continue the chain. The reaction starts only after the O2 is used up.

Q6. Give the products of cracking of propane.

Solution. C3H8 ⟶ CH4 + C2H4 (C–C homolysis then H-transfer) and C3H8 ⟶ C3H6 + H2.

★ 6.20 Very hard solved examples: halogenation and other alkane reactions

Q1. Monochlorination of 2,2,4-trimethylpentane (isooctane) at 25 °C (1° : 2° : 3° = 1 : 3.8 : 5). Give the % of each product and the number of stereoisomers.

Solution. H sets: C-1 (9 H, 1°) → 9; C-3 (2 H, 2°) → 7.6; C-4 (1 H, 3°) → 5; C-5 (6 H, 1°, the two CH3 on C-4) → 6. Total 27.6. 1-Chloro-2,2,4-trimethylpentane 32.6%; 3-chloro-2,2,4-trimethylpentane 27.5% (chiral, 2); 2-chloro-2,4,4-trimethylpentane 18.1%; 1-chloro-2,4,4-trimethylpentane 21.7% (chiral, 2). Six stereoisomers in all.

Q2. Repeat H1 for bromination (1 : 82 : 1600).

Solution. 9; 2 × 82 = 164; 1600; 6. Total 1779. 3° bromide (2-bromo-2,4,4-trimethylpentane) 89.9%, 2° 9.2%, C-1 0.5%, C-5 0.3%. Bromination is almost a one-product reaction.

Q3. Using ΔEₐ(1°–2°) = 3.3 kJ mol−1, predict the % of 2-chloropropane from propane at 300 °C (573 K). Compare with 25 °C.

Solution. k2/k1 = e3310/(8.314 × 573) = e0.695 = 2.00. % 2-chloro = 2 × 2.00 / (6 + 4.00) = 40% (at 25 °C it is 56%). Higher temperature → less selective.

Q4. Photochlorination of 1-chlorobutane gives about 6% 1,1-, 23% 1,2-, 46% 1,3- and 25% 1,4-dichlorobutane. Find the per-H reactivity of each position (C-4 = 1) and explain.

Solution. Per H: C-1 6/2 = 3; C-2 23/2 = 11.5; C-3 46/2 = 23; C-4 25/3 = 8.3. Relative to C-4: 0.36 : 1.4 : 2.8 : 1. In butane a CH2 is 3.8. The electronegative Cl makes nearby C–H electron-poor; Cl• is electrophilic, so attack at C-1 and C-2 is slowed (polar effect). [Percentages are typical literature values.]

Q5. (S)-1-Chloro-2-methylbutane is chlorinated (Cl2, hν). The 1,2-dichloro-2-methylbutane formed is optically inactive, but the 1,4-dichloro-2-methylbutane is optically active. Explain.

Solution. Attack at C-2 (the stereocentre, 3° H) gives a planar radical, so Cl adds from both faces: racemic. Attack at C-4 does not touch C-2, so its configuration is kept: optically active product. (H. C. Brown's classic test for planar radicals.)

Q6. How many monochloro products (constitutional and stereo) does 3-methylpentane give?

Solution. Four constitutional: 1-chloro-3-methylpentane (C-3 becomes a stereocentre: 2), 2-chloro-3-methylpentane (C-2 and C-3: 4), 3-chloro-3-methylpentane (1), 1-chloro-2-ethylbutane (from the 3-CH3; achiral: 1). Total 8 stereoisomers.

Q7. Light intensity in a photochlorination is made 9 times larger. By what factor does the rate change? Why not 9?

Solution. Rate ∝ I1/2 (6.2 h), so it rises 3 times. More light makes more Cl•, but termination (2Cl• → Cl2) grows with [Cl•]2, so [Cl•] grows only as I1/2.

Q8. For X• + CH4 ⟶ HX + •CH3 the values are: F (ΔH −130, Eₐ 5), Br (ΔH +73, Eₐ 75). Which TS is more product-like? Why can't Eₐ for I• be less than 141 kJ?

Solution. Br: Eₐ ≈ ΔH, so its TS is almost the products (late). F: TS is early. For an endothermic step the TS must lie at least as high as the products, so Eₐ ≥ ΔH = +141 kJ for I•.

Q9. Why can F2 + CH4 start without light, while Cl2 + CH4 cannot?

Solution. Molecule-assisted homolysis: F2 + H–CH3 ⟶ F• + HF + •CH3 has ΔH = 158 + 439 − 570 = +27 kJ, small enough at room temperature. For Cl2: 243 + 439 − 432 = +250 kJ: impossible without light.

Q10. NBS bromination of oct-1-ene gives two (actually three) monobromides. Give them.

Solution. Allylic H at C-3 is taken; the allyl radical C•H(C5H11)–CH=CH2 ⟷ C5H11CH=CH–CH2• reacts with Br2 at either end: 3-bromooct-1-ene (racemic) and 1-bromooct-2-ene as E and Z (mostly E).

Q11. An alkane C7H16 gives on bromination (Br2, hν, 127 °C) a 3° bromide almost exclusively, and on chlorination only 3 monochloro constitutional isomers. Identify it.

Solution. Only three kinds of H and at least one 3° H: 2,4-dimethylpentane, (CH3)2CH–CH2–CH(CH3)2: 12 equivalent 1° H, 2 equivalent 2° H, 2 equivalent 3° H. Bromination gives 2-bromo-2,4-dimethylpentane.

Q12. Chlorination of isobutane in neat alkane gives 3° : 1° per-H ≈ 4.5. In benzene solvent the ratio rises a lot. Explain using the reactivity–selectivity principle.

Solution. Cl• forms a π-complex with benzene, C6H6·Cl•. This complexed radical is less reactive, so its TS is later and feels more of the radical-stability difference: higher selectivity for the 3° H. (6.2 j)

Q13. Why does Cl2/hν on toluene give PhCH2Cl, while Cl2/FeCl3 in the dark gives o- and p-chlorotoluene?

Solution. Light makes Cl•, which takes the weak benzylic H (BDE ≈ 375) → PhCH2• → PhCH2Cl. FeCl3 makes the electrophile Cl+ (as FeCl4− complex), which attacks the ring (electrophilic aromatic substitution, o/p-directed by CH3). Same reagent, different mechanism.

Q14. In the chlorination of methane, why is CH3Cl more reactive towards Cl• than CH4 is, and how is polychlorination avoided?

Solution. The C–H of CH3Cl (≈ 419 kJ) is weaker than that of CH4 (439), because •CH2Cl is stabilised by a Cl lone pair. So CH2Cl2, CHCl3, CCl4 form readily. Using a large excess of CH4 keeps [CH3Cl] low, so Cl• mostly meets CH4.

Q15. Calculate ΔH for CH3CH3 + Br2 ⟶ CH3CH2Br + HBr using kJ values: C–H 420, Br–Br 193, C–Br 285, H–Br 366. Then give ΔH of each propagation step.

Solution. Step 1: 420 − 366 = +54. Step 2: 193 − 285 = −92. Overall = −38 kJ mol−1 (sum of the two steps).
